Decision Aware Origin-Destination Demand Estimation with Structurally Constrained Data

Xianzhe Wang    Yueyue Fan    Johannes O. Royset
Abstract

Origin-destination (OD) demand plays an important role in transportation system design and management applications. Conventional OD estimation methods typically judge estimation quality based on how estimated demand aligns with observed traffic data and historical demand patterns. We argue that data alignment alone is insufficient; how errors in OD estimates influence downstream decision quality should also be considered. This paper develops a decision aware OD demand estimation framework that leverages structurally constrained traffic data to characterize an admissible demand region, within which we identify OD estimates that would lead to least regret in the downstream decision. Therefore, our OD estimates are both data-consistent and decision-relevant. Methodologically, we approximate the admissible demand region induced by physical network constraints through a geometric representation, which regularizes the search over feasible OD estimates. Within this regularized region, we use a convex surrogate of downstream regret to obtain a tractable decision aware optimization problem. Numerical experiments show that the proposed framework consistently reduces decision regret relative to conventional estimation benchmarks, demonstrating the value of aligning OD demand estimation with downstream decision quality.

OD demand estimation; Decision aware; Structurally constrained data

1 Introduction

Travel demand serves as a critical parameter in almost all transportation system design and management applications, including traffic assignment, network design, congestion pricing, and infrastructure investment (Patriksson 2015, Yang and H. Bell 1998, De Palma and Lindsey 2011, Rokicki and Stępniak 2018). In the transportation science literature, the characterization and quantification of travel demand have long been central research objectives. Much of the existing literature on demand estimation focuses primarily on data alignment, where success is measured by how well estimated origin-destination (OD) flows conform to observed measurements or long-run covariates (Bierlaire and Crittin 2004, Krishnakumari et al. 2019, Demissie and Kattan 2022). In most transportation applications, OD demands are not ends in themselves, but rather intermediate inputs to downstream optimization, control, or policy design problems. Despite the central role of travel demand played in downstream applications, established methods for demand estimation remain decision agnostic. In this paper, we begin from the premise that the value of travel demand estimates lies in the quality of the decisions they support, not merely in their fidelity to observed data. Building on this premise, we introduce a new modeling framework for estimating the OD demand that is consistent with observed traffic conditions as well as its impact on the downstream decision-making objectives.

Existing travel demand estimation methods can be broadly categorized into two complementary paradigms: demand forecasting and demand reconstruction. Demand forecasting is for longer-term prediction and is typically grounded in the modeling of socioeconomic factors, such as household characteristics, economic activities, land use and accessibility. that give rise to travel demand (Jin et al. 2014, Pourebrahim et al. 2019, Yao et al. 2020, Yin et al. 2023). Demand reconstruction typically aims to infer an OD demand that best explains observed traffic conditions, thus often explicitly builds on network-based models. In this regard, our study fits better within the category of demand reconstruction, though our estimation framework leaves some flexibility to incorporate predictions from established behavioral models as prior information.

A major challenge in demand reconstruction lies in the underdetermined nature of the inverse network problem (Wang et al. 2023). Data consistency alone provides an incomplete basis for evaluating OD estimates, as multiple demand patterns may be equally compatible with observed measurements. A common approach to address the non-uniqueness of the inferred demand is to incorporate prior OD information, either for the complete set of OD pairs in a network (Cascetta 1984, Castillo et al. 2008) or for a partially observed subset of OD demands (Yang and Fan 2015). More broadly, uniqueness has been achieved by embedding additional structural preferences into the estimation problem, such as entropy maximization (Xie et al. 2011, Bar-Gera 2006), sparsity regularization (Wang et al. 2023), and statistical or dynamical assumptions (Maher 1983, Ros-Roca et al. 2022), which effectively shrink the feasible OD set and select a single admissible solution consistent with observed traffic data. All of these approaches are driven primarily by data alignment, with little consideration given to the quality of the downstream decisions that the resulting OD estimates are intended to support.

This paper presents a decision aware framework for OD estimation, shifting the focus from aligning estimates with data to aligning them with the performance of downstream decision-making tasks. To operationalize this decision awareness, we introduce decision regret as a bridge between OD estimation and downstream decision-making. Regret quantifies the loss in downstream objective value, had the estimated demand missed the “true” value. The concept of regret has been widely adopted in operations research as a principled criterion for assessing decision quality, particularly in evaluating the robustness and economic consequences of imperfect information (Bell 1983, Donti et al. 2017, Elmachtoub and Grigas 2022).

We consider a downstream optimization problem that depends on the OD demand ff. Let ℱ\mathcal{F} denote the feasible OD demand space, consisting of OD demand vectors that are consistent with the observed network data and satisfy basic feasibility constraints, such as nonnegativity and prescribed lower and upper bounds on OD demand. For any f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F}, let w⁡(f)∈arg⁡minw∈𝒲​f⊤​ww(f)\in\arg\min_{w\in\mathcal{W}}f^{\top}w denote an optimal downstream decision. Given the true OD demand ftruef_{\rm true}, the decision regret of an estimated demand ff is defined as

R⁡(ftrue,f)=ftrue⊤​w​(f)−minw∈𝒲⁡ftrue⊤​w.R(f_{\rm true},f)={f_{\rm true}}^{\top}w(f)-\min_{w\in\mathcal{W}}{f_{\rm true}}^{\top}w. (1)

Since ftruef_{\rm true} is unobserved in practice, we use the available prior demand as a proxy for ftruef_{\rm true} when constructing the regret criterion. The resulting formulation combines three key elements: link flow observations and feasibility constraints define the admissible OD space ℱ\mathcal{F}, the prior demand provides the reference for regret evaluation, and the downstream decision objective measures the performance of candidate OD estimates.

This research design departs from classical OD estimation in three ways. First, it replaces data fit as the primary criterion with downstream decision performance, directly linking OD estimation with downstream optimization. Second, it recognizes that OD estimation errors differ in their decision impact, giving greater weight to errors that are more consequential for downstream decisions. Third, this perspective treats the non-uniqueness of OD reconstruction not as a deficiency, but as an opportunity to select among feasible OD solutions based on their downstream decision performance.

Certainly, the new estimation framework also raises several challenges. The feasible OD demand space ℱ\mathcal{F} induced by structural constraints on the data can be high-dimensional and geometrically complex, while the regret function is generally nonconvex and thus computationally challenging to optimize. Moreover, directly optimizing a linear objective over ℱ\mathcal{F} tends to yield an extreme-point solution, which may be overly sensitive to sample-specific noise and thereby increase the risk of overfitting. To address these challenges, we develop a tractable decision aware estimation framework that uses geometric approximations of the feasible OD space to regularize estimation and mitigate sensitivity to extreme-point solutions, and replaces the nonconvex regret function with a convex surrogate. Exploiting duality, we reformulate the resulting problem as a convex quadratically constrained program, enabling scalable identification of structurally admissible OD estimates that support high-quality downstream decisions.

The main contributions of this study are as follows. From a conceptual perspective, we formally introduce a new problem formulation that systematically integrates structurally constrained OD reconstruction and downstream decision evaluation within a unified optimization framework. From a computational perspective, we develop a tractable and scalable decision aware estimation framework. The proposed approach comprises two key components: (i) a geometric ellipsoidal approximation of the structurally admissible OD demand space to address underdetermination and mitigate overfitting; (ii) a convex surrogate of the regret objective that preserves sensitivity to downstream decisions. From an empirical perspective, we develop a computationally efficient and scalable solution method and conduct extensive numerical experiments to validate the proposed framework. The results demonstrate that the decision aware OD estimates consistently yield lower regret in downstream decision problems compared with conventional methods, highlighting the practical value of aligning OD estimation objectives with decision performance.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 summarizes the current state of knowledge in the broader decision aware estimation literature, and identifies remaining gaps arising from unique challenges of transportation applications. Section 3 develops the decision aware OD estimation framework. It constructs a geometric approximation of the admissible OD demand space from structurally constrained data, formulates the corresponding decision aware estimation problem, and develops surrogate regret formulations that recast this problem as a tractable convex program. Section 4 presents numerical experiments on a range of network settings to evaluate the proposed approach in terms of downstream decision performance. Section 5 concludes with a discussion of implications and directions for future research.

2 Relation to the Broader Literature on Decision Aware Estimation

The use of downstream decision models, typically formulated as optimization problems, to inform estimation and learning has a long conceptual history and has attracted renewed attention in recent decades. As early as 1983, Bell (1983) introduces decision regret as a decision level concept based on counterfactual comparisons, laying the conceptual foundation for later decision-based evaluation frameworks, though not explicitly for estimation or prediction. Bengio (1997) articulates a decision centric learning paradigm, arguing that when downstream decision performance is the ultimate objective, minimizing prediction error is inherently suboptimal. Building on this insight, Kao et al. (2009) proposes directed regression, which explicitly embeds directional sensitivity induced by downstream objectives into the estimation process, thereby shifting the evaluation of estimation from standalone predictive accuracy to its consequences for downstream decision quality. Subsequent studies have shown the practical relevance of decision aware estimation across diverse domains, including operational planning, capacity management, and inventory control (Liyanage and Shanthikumar 2005, Bassamboo and Zeevi 2009, Akcay et al. 2011, Li et al. 2026), consistently finding that gains in predictive accuracy do not necessarily translate into improved decision quality.

In recent years, there has been a surge of interest in systematically incorporating downstream decision models into estimation and learning procedures. A canonical example is the Smart "Predict, then Optimize" (SPO) framework introduced by Elmachtoub and Grigas (2022). For optimization problems with uncertain linear objective coefficients, the framework introduces the SPO loss, which uses decision regret rather than traditional prediction losses (e.g., mean squared error) to penalize the downstream optimality gap, and admits a convex surrogate known as the SPO+ loss. In a sequence of subsequent studies, El Balghiti et al. (2023) establishes finite-sample generalization bounds for the SPO loss function. Building on this line of work, Loke et al. (2022) proposes a decision-driven regularization framework that provides a unifying perspective on balancing prediction accuracy and decision quality, with the SPO+ loss arising as a special case under specific choices of the regularization parameters. Mandi et al. (2020) demonstrates the empirical effectiveness of the SPO+ loss across a range of combinatorial optimization problems. Beyond seeking surrogate losses for decision regret, a broad stream of work aims to directly approximate the sensitivity of downstream decisions with respect to predicted parameters. Specifically, this line of research focuses on estimating the gradient ∂w∂f\frac{\partial w}{\partial f} and leveraging this information to capture how changes in the predictive model affect downstream decisions. The resulting sensitivity information is then used to guide the parameter updates of the estimation model. Some studies restrict attention to structured classes of optimization problems. For example, Amos and Kolter (2017) consider convex quadratic programs and obtain analytical expressions for the decision gradients by differentiating through the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions via the implicit function theorem. Related approaches have been developed for conic optimization problems (Agrawal et al. 2019). However, for general optimization problems, this gradient-based paradigm faces a fundamental challenge because the mapping from problem parameters to optimal decisions can be nonsmooth or unstable; see, for example, Section 5.A of Royset and Wets (2021) for a discussion of the instability of minimizers. In many discrete optimization problems, this mapping is piecewise constant, implying that the corresponding derivatives are zero almost everywhere and undefined at the remaining points. To address this issue, existing approaches introduce regularization to construct a surrogate for the decision gradient (Wilder et al. 2019, Mandi and Guns 2020). Beyond explicitly regularizing the optimization objective, several studies adopt a probabilistic perspective and introduce implicit regularization through randomized decision mappings. In this line of work, the mapping from predictions ff to decisions ww is modeled as a function that induces a probability distribution over the feasible region 𝒲\mathcal{W}, so that w⁡(f)w(f) can be interpreted as a random variable conditional on ff. This formulation enables gradient estimation via perturbation-based sampling schemes (Pogančić et al. 2019, Blondel et al. 2020). A substantial body of subsequent work has examined the statistical properties, surrogate loss constructions, and computational tractability of decision aware objectives, with demonstrated applicability to a broad class of downstream decision problems. We refer the reader to recent survey papers in this area for a comprehensive overview (Sadana et al. 2025, Mandi et al. 2024, Qi and Shen 2022).

Limitations and gaps in transportation applications.

While these paradigms have substantially advanced the integration of estimation and optimization, they remain fundamentally misaligned with the structure of transportation network-level OD demand estimation problems. Here, OD demand estimation is characterized by high-dimensional feasible demand sets induced by physical network constraints, flow conservation, and behavioral assumptions, together with limited and indirect observations. In such settings, OD demand is generically non-identifiable: many distinct demand patterns are observationally equivalent, yet can give rise to sharply different downstream decisions. Existing decision aware approaches, however, largely retain a point estimation perspective, implicitly framing estimation as the recovery of a single latent “true” parameter vector and interpreting decision losses as the consequence of small, local deviations around this point. This viewpoint is ill-suited to OD estimation, where uncertainty is not concentrated around a neighborhood of a unique solution, but is distributed over a large, structured feasible region. The proposed framework integrates structurally constrained OD estimation with decision aware optimization to fill the gaps.

3 Decision Aware OD Estimation Framework

This section develops a decision aware framework for OD demand estimation in transportation networks. In Section 3.1, we characterize the structurally underdetermined OD estimation problem induced by network flow constraints and construct a tractable ellipsoidal approximation of the admissible OD space. Building on this geometric representation, in Section 3.2, we then formulate a decision aware OD estimation framework that explicitly incorporates downstream optimization problems and defines estimation objectives in terms of expected downstream decision regret under a given error distribution of the true demand. Section 3.3 introduces a convex surrogate for the generally nonconvex regret objective, yielding tractable surrogate regret formulations. Finally, Section 3.4 derives deterministic equivalent reformulations of the resulting models, showing that the formulation over the original feasible OD region reduces to a linear program, whereas its ellipsoidal counterpart admits an equivalent convex quadratically constrained programming formulation.

3.1 Geometric Approximation from Structurally Constrained Data

A defining feature of transportation systems is that many observed quantities are governed by physical conservation laws imposed by the network structure. In particular, when traffic moves through a fixed set of links and originates from a collection of OD pairs, the relationship between link flows and OD flows is fully encoded by the link-OD incidence matrix. Let X∈ℝm×nX\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} denote this matrix, where mm is the number of directed links and nn is the number of OD pairs. Given a vector of reliable link-flow measurements L∈ℝmL\in\mathbb{R}^{m}, the underlying OD flow vector f∈ℝnf\in\mathbb{R}^{n} must satisfy the fundamental physical constraint

L=X​f.L=Xf. (2)

Equation (2) captures the conservation of vehicles on every link of the network: the total number of vehicles that traverse a link must equal the aggregate contributions of all OD pairs that utilize that link.

For realistic networks, the number of OD pairs far exceeds the number of links, i.e., n≫mn\gg m. Consequently, the system of equations in (2) is underdetermined. For any observed link-flow vector LL, there exist infinitely many estimators for ff, but they must respect the feasible set defined by (2). Put differently, even though the OD flows are unobserved and often highly uncertain, they are never arbitrary: they are restricted to lie within the affine subspace of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} determined by the measured link flows and the physical network structure.

For a linear system X​f=LXf=L where XX is rank deficient ( n≫mn\gg m ), we highlight two remarks that are directly relevant to this study. First, when X⊤​XX^{\top}X is nonsingular (the full rank case), Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse X+X^{+} is equivalent to X+=(X⊤​X)−1​X⊤X^{+}=(X^{\top}X)^{-1}X^{\top}, where X−1X^{-1} is the ordinary inverse of matrix XX. Second, the solution X+​LX^{+}L, calculated based on the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse, has the minimum length among all feasible solutions to X​f=LXf=L (see Fan and Kalaba (2003), Rao and Mitra (1971) for more comprehensive discussions). Within the broader feasible OD demand space ℱ\mathcal{F}, we consider the subset SS characterized by consistency with the observed link flows. With this notation, the full solution set to the normal equation is

S=X+​L+ker⁡(X⊤​X)=(X+​L+{v∈ℝn:X⊤​X​v=0}CLOSE.S=X^{+}L+\ker(X^{\top}X)=(X^{+}L\;+\;\{\,v\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:X^{\top}Xv=0\,\}. (3)

This decomposition reveals that all feasible OD flow vectors consist of a canonical minimum norm solution plus an arbitrary vector in the nullspace of X⊤​XX^{\top}X, which captures all OD flow directions that do not affect the observed link flows.

Let q=rank⁡(X)q=\operatorname{rank}(X) and let f¯=X+​L\bar{f}=X^{+}L denote the particular least squares solution. We express the feasible set for the demand estimator as

S′={f¯+Vz∣ 0≤f¯+Vz≤U,z∈ℝn−q},S^{\prime}=\{\;\bar{f}+Vz\;\mid\;0\leq\bar{f}+Vz\leq U,z\in\mathbb{R}^{n-q}\;\},

where V∈ℝn×(n−q)V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(n-q)} is the matrix whose columns form an orthonormal basis for ker⁡(X⊤​X)\ker(X^{\top}X), and UU sets an upper bound. This representation follows directly from the fact that the nullspace of X⊤​XX^{\top}X contains all directions that leave the link flows unchanged; hence, any feasible ff differs from f¯\bar{f} only through motions in this subspace.

In a meaningful size of network problem, the feasible region S′S^{\prime} constitutes a high-dimensional polyhedral set. Because direct characterization of its size and shape is computationally intractable, we approximate this feasible region by an ellipsoid, which provides a tractable representation of its geometric extent and uncertainty. Following the approach of Renegar (2001) and Chen et al. (2006), we construct an ellipsoidal approximation centered at the analytic-center of S′S^{\prime}. Let z⋆z^{\star} denote the analytic-center parameter, defined by the solution to the logarithmic barrier problem

minz−∑i=1n[log⁡(Ui−f¯i−(V​z)i)+log⁡(f¯i+(V​z)i)].\min_{z}\;-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Bigl[\log(U_{i}-\bar{f}_{i}-(Vz)_{i})\;+\;\log(\bar{f}_{i}+(Vz)_{i})\Bigr].

For notational simplicity, define the vector g⁡(z)=f¯+V​zg(z)=\bar{f}+Vz, so that the objective becomes ϕ(z)=−∑i=1n[log(Ui−gi(z))+log(gi(z))]\phi(z)=-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Bigl[\log(U_{i}-g_{i}(z))+\log(g_{i}(z))\Bigr].

Let HH be the Hessian of ϕ⁡(z)\phi(z) at z⋆z^{\star}. Since g⁡(z)=f¯+V​zg(z)=\bar{f}+Vz is affine, its Jacobian is VV, and the Hessian takes the explicit form

H=V⊤​[diag⁡(1gi​(z⋆)2+1(Ui−gi​(z⋆))2)]​V.H=V^{\top}\left[\mathrm{diag}\!\left(\frac{1}{g_{i}(z^{\star})^{2}}+\frac{1}{(U_{i}-g_{i}(z^{\star}))^{2}}\right)\right]V.

This Hessian defines the local curvature of the logarithmic barrier and yields a natural ellipsoidal approximation of S′S^{\prime} centered at the analytic-center f⋆=g⁡(z⋆)f^{\star}=g(z^{\star}). Following Renegar (2001), define the HH-norm ball B⁡(z⋆,r)={z|(z−z⋆)⊤​H​(z−z⋆)≤r2}B(z^{\star},r)=\bigl\{z\;\bigm|\;(z-z^{\star})^{\top}H(z-z^{\star})\leq r^{2}\bigr\}. Renegar’s analysis establishes that, for self-concordant logarithmic barriers,

B⁡(z⋆,1)⊆{z∣0≤f¯+V​z≤U}⊆B⁡(z⋆,4​ν+1),B(z^{\star},1)\;\subseteq\;\{\,z\mid 0\leq\bar{f}+Vz\leq U\,\}\;\subseteq\;B(z^{\star},4\nu+1),

where ν\nu is the complexity parameter of the barrier function. In our case, the barrier consists of 2​n2n logarithmic terms, and therefore ν=2​n\nu=2n.

Mapping these sets back to the OD flow space via the affine transformation f=f¯+V​zf=\bar{f}+Vz yields f¯+V​B​(z⋆,1)⊆S′⊆f¯+V​B​(z⋆,4​ν+1)\bar{f}+VB(z^{\star},1)\;\subseteq\;S^{\prime}\;\subseteq\;\bar{f}+VB(z^{\star},4\nu+1). Since VV acts only on the displacement variable, we also have the equivalent representation f¯+V​B​(z⋆,r)=f⋆+V​B​(0,r)\bar{f}+VB(z^{\star},r)=f^{\star}+VB(0,r). This ellipsoidal sandwiched approximation provides a computationally tractable geometric surrogate for the true feasible set S′S^{\prime}. Figure 1 geometrically illustrates how the OD flow uncertainty set emerges from the nullspace of the link–OD incidence matrix and how the ellipsoidal approximation captures the feasible variation directions.

The representation f=f¯+V​zf=\bar{f}+Vz highlights that all admissible OD flows in S′S^{\prime} differ only through movements in the nullspace directions encoded by zz. These directions do not affect the physical constraint L=X​fL=Xf, since X​V=0XV=0, and, when zz remains within the ball B⁡(0,r)B(0,r), the resulting ff automatically respects the box constraints 0≤f≤U0\leq f\leq U. Thus, zz captures the “degrees of freedom” available for adjusting ff without violating either the physical conservation constraints or the OD bounds. This flexibility allows downstream decision models to choose zz in a way that optimizes performance while remaining within the feasible ellipsoidal region.

In particular, the ellipsoidal constraint

z⊤​H​z≤r2,z^{\top}Hz\leq r^{2}, (4)

where r≥1r\geq 1 controls the radius of the search region, provides a compact and tractable characterization of the controllable degrees of freedom available for downstream optimization. The choice r=1r=1 guarantees that the ellipsoid is contained in S′S^{\prime}. As the nullspace dimension grows, however, the unit ellipsoid may capture only a small portion of the admissible OD variation and thus become overly conservative. We therefore treat rr as a tuning parameter: increasing rr expands the ellipsoidal search region and allows a broader range of decision-relevant demand patterns to be explored. Although r>1r>1 relinquishes the automatic containment guarantee, the nullspace construction continues to preserve flow conservation because X​V=0XV=0; only the lower and upper bounds on OD demand may be violated. Such violations can be tolerated when modest, while the original bounds can be imposed explicitly whenever strict feasibility is required. Appendix A analyzes the effect of nullspace dimension and discusses the calibration of rr.

This controlled expansion is useful for decision aware estimation because the goal is to reduce downstream regret rather than preserve statistical fidelity alone. The resulting estimate therefore need not be unbiased, and small violations of the data-derived OD bounds may be justified if they improve downstream decisions. For example, suppose an intervention is triggered when estimated demand exceeds 25. If failing to intervene when actual demand exceeds this threshold is more costly than intervening unnecessarily, a modest upward bias near the threshold may be preferable to a comparable downward bias. A larger rr provides the flexibility for such decision driven adjustments, while the regret objective determines their direction and magnitude.

3.2 Optimization Formulation for Decision Aware OD Estimation

Consider the following decision problem that takes OD flow ff as an input:

minw∈𝒲⁡f⊤​w,\min_{w\in\mathcal{W}}f^{\top}w, (5)

where ww denotes the downstream decision and 𝒲\mathcal{W} is a nonempty compact polyhedron defined by the linear operational constraints of the downstream problem. We denote the optimal objective value of this problem by c⁡(f)=minw∈𝒲⁡f⊤​wc(f)=\min_{w\in\mathcal{W}}f^{\top}w, and denote by w⁡(f)∈arg⁡minw∈𝒲​f⊤​ww(f)\in\arg\min_{w\in\mathcal{W}}f^{\top}w an optimal decision under ff. Note that, by duality, ff can equivalently appear either as coefficients in the objective function or as right-hand-side constants in the constraints. This formulation captures many transportation applications in which OD flows drive payoffs, costs, or service levels, including assignment problems (e.g., allocating vehicles to OD pairs), matching problems (e.g., pairing demand and supply across zones), and transportation or freight flow problems with fixed capacity constraints.

If the true OD flow is ftruef_{\rm true} but the downstream optimization problem is solved using an estimated OD flow vector ff, the resulting decision generally yields a suboptimal objective value. The associated loss is measured by the regret defined in (1), which captures the degradation in decision quality induced by OD estimation error. In practice, ftruef_{\rm true} is fixed but unobserved. Suppose that prior information provides an estimate f0f_{0} of the true OD flow. We model the unknown discrepancy between f0f_{0} and ftruef_{\rm true} by a random error ε\varepsilon with distribution 𝒫\mathcal{P}, and represent the uncertain true OD flow as

F=f0+ε,ε∼𝒫.F=f_{0}+\varepsilon,\qquad\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{P}.

Here, f0f_{0} is fixed and observed, whereas ε\varepsilon and hence FF are random. For now, we assume that the error distribution 𝒫\mathcal{P} is known. Appendix B describes how 𝒫\mathcal{P} can be constructed from historical prediction residuals and contextual information, including historical demand and socioeconomic features.

Decision aWare Estimation (DWE) therefore seeks to minimize the expected regret under the uncertainty in the true OD flow:

ming⁡(z)∈S′⁡𝔼ε∼𝒫​[R⁡(f0+ε,g⁡(z))].\min_{g(z)\in S^{\prime}}\;\mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{P}}\left[R\bigl(f_{0}+\varepsilon,\;g(z)\bigr)\right]. (DWE-original)

Recall that S′S^{\prime} is the feasible OD set induced by link-flow conservation and OD bounds, and that g⁡(z)=f¯+V​zg(z)=\bar{f}+Vz parameterizes a candidate OD estimate in S′S^{\prime}.

Within the ellipsoidal approximation of the feasible region, the DWE formulation becomes

minz:z⊤​H​z≤r2𝔼ε∼𝒫[R(f0+ε,g(z))].\min_{z:z^{\top}Hz\leq r^{2}}\;\mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{P}}\left[R\bigl(f_{0}+\varepsilon,\;g(z)\bigr)\right]. (DWE-Ellipsoid)

For applications where tail risk plays an important role, a more conservative formulation replaces the expectation with the superquantile, also known as Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR), where β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1) denotes the confidence level:

minz:z⊤​H​z≤r2CVaRβ,ε∼𝒫[R(f0+ε,g(z))].\min_{z:z^{\top}Hz\leq r^{2}}\;\mathrm{CVaR}_{\beta,\,\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{P}}\left[R\bigl(f_{0}+\varepsilon,\;g(z)\bigr)\right]. (6)

3.3 Surrogate Regret Formulations

The regret defined in (1) is generally nonconvex in the estimated OD flow ff. Therefore, directly minimizing its expectation or a risk measure with respect to ff (or equivalently with respect to zz through f=f¯+V​zf=\bar{f}+Vz) leads to a nonconvex optimization problem.

Elmachtoub and Grigas (2022) shows that, for linear optimization problems, the regret admits a tractable convex upper bound known as the SPO++ loss. We follow their construction and retain the auxiliary scaling parameter α>0\alpha>0 that arises in the derivation of the SPO++ upper bound, yielding a parameterized surrogate denoted by ℓα\ell_{\alpha}. We discuss the role and choice of α\alpha later in this section. Let f∗f^{\ast} denote a realization of the uncertain true OD flow F=f0+εF=f_{0}+\varepsilon. Given f∗f^{\ast} and a candidate OD estimate ff, the parameterized surrogate is defined as

ℓα​(f∗,f):=maxw∈𝒲⁡(f∗−α​f)⊤​w+α​f⊤​w​(f∗)−f∗⊤​w​(f∗).\ell_{\alpha}(f^{\ast},f):=\max_{w\in\mathcal{W}}(f^{\ast}-\alpha f)^{\top}w+\alpha f^{\top}w(f^{\ast})-{f^{\ast}}^{\top}w(f^{\ast}). (7)

The following proposition summarizes the properties of ℓα\ell_{\alpha} in our notation. Appendix C provides the proof.

Proposition 3.1 (Properties of ℓα\ell_{\alpha})

For any α>0\alpha>0 and any realized OD flow vector f∗f^{\ast}, the surrogate ℓα\ell_{\alpha} satisfies:

  1. 1.

    Upper bound on regret:

    R⁡(f∗,f)≤ℓα​(f∗,f)for all ​f∈ℝn;R(f^{\ast},f)\;\leq\;\ell_{\alpha}(f^{\ast},f)\qquad\text{for all }f\in\mathbb{R}^{n};
  2. 2.

    Convexity: ℓα​(f∗,f)\ell_{\alpha}(f^{\ast},f) is a convex function of ff;

  3. 3.

    Subgradient: for any ff,

    α⁡(w⁡(f∗)−w⁡(α​f−f∗))∈∂fℓα​(f∗,f).\alpha\bigl(w(f^{\ast})-w(\alpha f-f^{\ast})\bigr)\;\in\;\partial_{f}\,\ell_{\alpha}(f^{\ast},f).

Proposition 3.1 establishes several fundamental properties of the ℓα\ell_{\alpha} surrogate, including its tractability and its ability to provide an upper bound on the true regret associated with a downstream linear decision problem.

The classical SPO++ construction of Elmachtoub and Grigas (2022) sets α=2\alpha=2 because, within the empirical risk minimization (ERM) framework, this choice yields a convex surrogate that is Fisher consistent, meaning that, under the stated conditions, minimizing the population SPO++ risk also minimizes the true SPO risk. However, our approach does not rely on such distributional consistency. Rather than learning a direct prediction ff through ERM, we optimize the parameterized surrogate over a physically constrained feasible OD space. Under this paradigm, the desirable value of α\alpha is not dictated by Fisher consistency of an ERM estimator, but by the quality of the resulting surrogate and its downstream decision performance, thereby allowing greater flexibility in its choice.

The surrogate objective ℓα​(f∗,f)\ell_{\alpha}(f^{\ast},f) is affected by two distinct sources of discrepancy: (i) surrogate approximation, arising from replacing the original regret with a tractable convex upper bound; and (ii) uncertainty perturbation, arising because the surrogate is evaluated at a realization f∗f^{\ast} of the uncertain OD flow rather than at the unobserved true flow ftruef_{\rm true}. These two effects interact with the choice of α\alpha. The following proposition provides an explicit bound that characterizes this tradeoff.

Proposition 3.2 (Tradeoff Bound for the ℓα\ell_{\alpha} Surrogate)

Let f∗f^{\ast} be a realization of the uncertain OD flow FF. Suppose that 𝒲\mathcal{W} is compact and that there exist constants U>0U>0 and Bw>0B_{w}>0 such that ‖f‖,‖f∗‖,‖ftrue‖≤U\|f\|,\|f^{\ast}\|,\|f_{\rm true}\|\leq U and ‖w‖≤Bw\|w\|\leq B_{w} for all w∈𝒲w\in\mathcal{W}. Further suppose that, for the candidate OD estimate ff, there exists κ>0\kappa>0 such that f⊤​(w−w⁡(f))≥κ​‖w−w⁡(f)‖f^{\top}(w-w(f))\geq\kappa\|w-w(f)\| for all w∈𝒲w\in\mathcal{W}.

For any α>0\alpha>0, the discrepancy between the surrogate and the true regret admits the decomposition

ℓα​(f∗,f)−R⁡(ftrue,f)=ℓα​(ftrue,f)−R⁡(ftrue,f)⏟surrogate approximation+ℓα​(f∗,f)−ℓα​(ftrue,f)⏟uncertainty perturbation.\ell_{\alpha}(f^{\ast},f)-R(f_{\rm true},f)=\underbrace{\ell_{\alpha}(f_{\rm true},f)-R(f_{\rm true},f)}_{\text{surrogate approximation}}+\underbrace{\ell_{\alpha}(f^{\ast},f)-\ell_{\alpha}(f_{\rm true},f)}_{\text{uncertainty perturbation}}.

Moreover,

ℓα​(f∗,f)−R⁡(ftrue,f)≤2​U2​Bwκ​α+2​α​Bw​(‖f−ftrue‖+‖f∗−f‖)+2​Bw​‖f∗−ftrue‖.\ell_{\alpha}(f^{\ast},f)-R(f_{\rm true},f)\leq\frac{2U^{2}B_{w}}{\kappa\alpha}+2\alpha B_{w}\left(\|f-f_{\rm true}\|+\|f^{\ast}-f\|\right)+2B_{w}\|f^{\ast}-f_{\rm true}\|. (8)

If ‖f−ftrue‖+‖f∗−f‖>0\|f-f_{\rm true}\|+\|f^{\ast}-f\|>0, the α\alpha-dependent part of the bound is minimized at

α∗=Uκ⁡(‖f−ftrue‖+‖f∗−f‖).\alpha^{\ast}=\frac{U}{\sqrt{\kappa\left(\|f-f_{\rm true}\|+\|f^{\ast}-f\|\right)}}. (9)

The detailed proof is given in Appendix D.

Discussion.

Proposition 3.2 shows that α\alpha balances surrogate approximation against sensitivity to OD flow discrepancies. In (8), the approximation term decreases as 1/α1/\alpha, whereas the discrepancy-dependent term increases linearly with α\alpha. Hence, a small α\alpha yields a looser regret approximation, while a large α\alpha makes the surrogate more sensitive to differences among the candidate, realized, and true OD flows. The remaining uncertainty term is independent of α\alpha. Equation (9) summarizes this balance. Larger OD-flow discrepancies favor a smaller α\alpha because their contribution to the bound is amplified linearly by α\alpha. In contrast, a smaller κ\kappa favors a larger α\alpha: when the downstream optimum is less sharply separated, a larger scaling factor is needed to control the surrogate-approximation term. Since ftruef_{\rm true} is unobserved, α∗\alpha^{\ast} serves as an oracle benchmark; in practice, α\alpha is selected based on downstream decision performance in Section 4.

By replacing R⁡(f0+ε,g⁡(z))R(f_{0}+\varepsilon,g(z)) in the objectives of (DWE-original) and (DWE-Ellipsoid) with its convex surrogate ℓα​(f0+ε,g⁡(z))\ell_{\alpha}(f_{0}+\varepsilon,g(z)), and noting that g⁡(z)=f¯+V​zg(z)=\bar{f}+Vz is affine in zz, the resulting optimization problems are convex in zz and can be solved using standard convex optimization methods.

Theorem 3.3 (Convexity and Subgradient of the Expectation Formulation)

Let H∈ℝd×dH\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} be positive definite, and consider

minz∈ℝd:z⊤​H​z≤r2ϕ(z):=𝔼ε∼𝒫[ℓα(f0+ε,g(z))].\min_{z\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\;z^{\top}Hz\leq r^{2}}\phi(z):=\mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{P}}\left[\ell_{\alpha}(f_{0}+\varepsilon,g(z))\right].

Assume that ℓα​(f0+ε,g⁡(z))\ell_{\alpha}(f_{0}+\varepsilon,g(z)) is integrable for every feasible zz, and that the subgradient expression below is integrable with respect to ε∼𝒫\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{P}. Then:

  1. 1.

    ϕ⁡(z)\phi(z) is convex in zz, and the optimization problem is a convex optimization problem;

  2. 2.

    a subgradient of ϕ\phi at zz is given by

    𝔼ε∼𝒫​[α​V⊤​(w⁡(f0+ε)−w⁡(α​g​(z)−f0−ε))]∈∂ϕ⁡(z).\mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{P}}\left[\alpha V^{\top}\left(w(f_{0}+\varepsilon)-w\bigl(\alpha g(z)-f_{0}-\varepsilon\bigr)\right)\right]\in\partial\phi(z).

Theorem 3.3 shows that the expectation formulation is a convex optimization problem. Since ℓα​(f∗,f)\ell_{\alpha}(f^{\ast},f) is convex but generally nonsmooth in its second argument, ϕ⁡(z)\phi(z) is convex and may also be nondifferentiable. By Proposition 3.1, for each realization f0+εf_{0}+\varepsilon, a subgradient with respect to the second argument is α⁡[w⁡(f0+ε)−w⁡(α​g​(z)−f0−ε)]\alpha[w(f_{0}+\varepsilon)-w(\alpha g(z)-f_{0}-\varepsilon)]. Since g⁡(z)g(z) is affine, multiplication by V⊤V^{\top} gives the corresponding subgradient with respect to zz, and taking expectations yields the expression in Theorem 3.3. An analogous argument applies to CVaR; see Appendix F for a formal statement and proof.

3.4 Equivalent Reformulations and Computational Solution

We next show that the surrogate DWE formulations admit standard deterministic optimization reformulations and can therefore be solved directly using off-the-shelf optimization software. To obtain a finite-dimensional computational representation, we approximate the prior distribution of the true OD flow by a discrete scenario distribution. Specifically, let τk:=f0+εk\tau_{k}:=f_{0}+\varepsilon_{k}, k=1,…,Kk=1,\ldots,K, denote the representative OD-flow realizations, with associated probabilities pkp_{k}, where ∑k=1Kpk=1\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_{k}=1. This yields the discrete approximation 𝒫^=∑k=1Kpk​δτk\widehat{\mathcal{P}}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_{k}\,\delta_{\tau_{k}}, where δτk\delta_{\tau_{k}} denotes a point mass at τk\tau_{k}. We further define w¯:=𝔼τ∼𝒫^​[w⁡(τ)]=∑k=1Kpk​w​(τk),\bar{w}:=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\widehat{\mathcal{P}}}[w(\tau)]=\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_{k}w(\tau_{k}),, which is the probability-weighted average of the optimal downstream decisions induced by the prior OD-flow realizations.

Under the finite-scenario representation of the prior distribution, substituting the definition of ℓα​(τk,f)\ell_{\alpha}(\tau_{k},f) in (7) yields

∑k=1Kpk​ℓα​(τk,f)=\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_{k}\,\ell_{\alpha}(\tau_{k},f)= ∑k=1Kpk​maxw∈𝒲​(τk−α​f)⊤​w+α​f⊤​w¯−∑k=1Kpk​τk⊤​w​(τk).\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_{k}\max_{w\in\mathcal{W}}(\tau_{k}-\alpha f)^{\top}w+\alpha f^{\top}\bar{w}-\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_{k}\,\tau_{k}^{\top}w(\tau_{k}). (10)

The last term is independent of the estimation decision ff and can therefore be omitted without affecting the optimizer.

We now exploit the linear structure of the downstream decision problem. Suppose that its feasible region admits the general polyhedral representation

𝒲={w∈ℝn:Aw≤b,Bw=d},\mathcal{W}=\left\{w\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:Aw\leq b,\;Bw=d\right\},

where the equality constraints capture, for example, flow-conservation or balance requirements, while capacity constraints, resource restrictions, and variable bounds can be incorporated into A​w≤bAw\leq b.

For each prior scenario kk, the inner optimization problem is therefore

maxw{(τk−αf)⊤w:Aw≤b,Bw=d}.\max_{w}\left\{(\tau_{k}-\alpha f)^{\top}w:Aw\leq b,\;Bw=d\right\}.

Let λk≥0\lambda_{k}\geq 0 denote the dual variables associated with the inequality constraints and let μk\mu_{k} denote the unrestricted dual variables associated with the equality constraints. Assuming the downstream problem is feasible and bounded, strong linear programming duality gives

maxw{(τk−αf)⊤w:Aw≤b,Bw=d}=minλk≥0,μk{b⊤λk+d⊤μk:A⊤λk+B⊤μk=τk−αf}.\max_{w}\left\{(\tau_{k}-\alpha f)^{\top}w:Aw\leq b,\;Bw=d\right\}=\min_{\lambda_{k}\geq 0,\;\mu_{k}}\left\{b^{\top}\lambda_{k}+d^{\top}\mu_{k}:A^{\top}\lambda_{k}+B^{\top}\mu_{k}=\tau_{k}-\alpha f\right\}.

Thus, the nested optimization in the surrogate loss can be eliminated, yielding a single-level deterministic equivalent formulation.

For the original feasible OD region S′S^{\prime}, DWE-original is equivalent, up to an additive constant independent of the decision variables, to

minf,{λk,μk}k=1K\displaystyle\min_{f,\{\lambda_{k},\mu_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K}} α​f⊤​w¯+∑k=1Kpk​(b⊤​λk+d⊤​μk)\displaystyle\alpha f^{\top}\bar{w}+\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_{k}\left(b^{\top}\lambda_{k}+d^{\top}\mu_{k}\right) (DWE-original-DE)
s.t.\displaystyle\text{s.t.} A⊤​λk+B⊤​μk=τk−α​f,\displaystyle A^{\top}\lambda_{k}+B^{\top}\mu_{k}=\tau_{k}-\alpha f, k=1,…,K,\displaystyle k=1,\ldots,K,
λk≥0,\displaystyle\lambda_{k}\geq 0, k=1,…,K,\displaystyle k=1,\ldots,K,
X​f=L,\displaystyle Xf=L,
0≤f≤U.\displaystyle 0\leq f\leq U.

The objective and all constraints in DWE-original-DE are linear. Hence, the finite-scenario surrogate formulation of DWE-original is a linear program.

The same dual reformulation applies to DWE-Ellipsoid. Substituting f=g⁡(z)=f¯+V​zf=g(z)=\bar{f}+Vz yields

minz,{λk,μk}k=1K\displaystyle\min_{z,\{\lambda_{k},\mu_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K}} α​(f¯+V​z)⊤​w¯+∑k=1Kpk​(b⊤​λk+d⊤​μk)\displaystyle\alpha(\bar{f}+Vz)^{\top}\bar{w}+\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_{k}\left(b^{\top}\lambda_{k}+d^{\top}\mu_{k}\right) (DWE-Ellipsoid-DE)
s.t.\displaystyle\text{s.t.} A⊤​λk+B⊤​μk=τk−α⁡(f¯+V​z),\displaystyle A^{\top}\lambda_{k}+B^{\top}\mu_{k}=\tau_{k}-\alpha(\bar{f}+Vz), k=1,…,K,\displaystyle k=1,\ldots,K,
λk≥0,\displaystyle\lambda_{k}\geq 0, k=1,…,K,\displaystyle k=1,\ldots,K,
z⊤​H​z≤r2.\displaystyle z^{\top}Hz\leq r^{2}.

Since H≻0H\succ 0, the ellipsoidal constraint is convex, while the objective and all remaining constraints are linear. Thus, DWE-Ellipsoid-DE can be viewed as a special case of a convex quadratically constrained quadratic program (QCQP), with a linear objective function and a single convex quadratic constraint. Moreover, letting H=R⊤​RH=R^{\top}R denote a Cholesky factorization, the ellipsoidal constraint can equivalently be expressed as ‖R​z‖2≤r\|Rz\|_{2}\leq r. Hence, DWE-Ellipsoid-DE also admits an equivalent second-order cone programming (SOCP) representation.

The resulting formulations belong to standard classes of convex optimization problems. DWE-original-DE reduces to an LP, whereas DWE-Ellipsoid-DE can be formulated as either a convex QCQP or an SOCP. Both formulations can be handled directly by modern optimization solvers, thereby avoiding the need for a customized nonsmooth optimization algorithm.

4 Numerical Experiments

Numerical experiments based on three test networks of varying sizes are conducted to test and validate the proposed decision aware OD estimation framework. Besides checking the accuracy and scalability of our method, we also examine how decision regret varies with model misspecification and data noise, and show that the proposed framework effectively reduces decision error and adapts the surrogate parameter α\alpha as the error structure changes.

4.1 An Illustrative Toy Example for Motivating Decision-awareness

This simple numerical example is designed to motivate the need for decision awareness and to illustrate the interaction between various pulling sources, including prior information presented by historical samples, physical feasibility based on current sensor observations, and downstream decision quality, in an underdetermined OD estimation problem.

Consider a toy network with three nodes, three OD flows, and two directed links, as shown in Figure 2. Let f=(f12,f23,f13)⊤f=(f_{12},f_{23},f_{13})^{\top} denote the OD demand vector. Suppose that only link (1,2)(1,2) is instrumented with a sensor, and the observed link flow is L12=100.L_{12}=100. Under the path structure in Figure 2, this observation implies the linear constraint f12+f13=100.f_{12}+f_{13}=100. In addition, assume simple capacity bounds 0≤f12,f23,f13≤200.0\leq f_{12},f_{23},f_{13}\leq 200. These constraints form the feasible OD set, and any point within this feasible set aligns with the observed data.

Now let us illustrate how OD estimation affects downstream decisions. Consider the following simple decision problem:

min𝐰∈ℝ3\displaystyle\min_{\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}} f12​w1+f23​w2+f13​w3\displaystyle f_{12}w_{1}+f_{23}w_{2}+f_{13}w_{3} (11)
s.t.\displaystyle\text{s.t.} w1+w2+w3=1,\displaystyle w_{1}+w_{2}+w_{3}=1,
w1−w3=0,\displaystyle w_{1}-w_{3}=0,
0≤w1,w2,w3≤1.\displaystyle 0\leq w_{1},w_{2},w_{3}\leq 1.

With symmetry between w1w_{1} and w3w_{3}, problem (11) reduces to comparing two effective actions. The derived decision rule is

{w=(0,1,0),if ​f23≤f12+f132,w=(12,0,12),if ​f23>f12+f132.\begin{cases}w=(0,1,0),&\text{if }f_{23}\leq\dfrac{f_{12}+f_{13}}{2},\\[6.0pt] w=\left(\dfrac{1}{2},0,\dfrac{1}{2}\right),&\text{if }f_{23}>\dfrac{f_{12}+f_{13}}{2}.\end{cases}

For OD estimates that satisfy the sensor information f12+f13=100f_{12}+f_{13}=100, this decision boundary reduces to f23=50f_{23}=50. Therefore, the downstream action depends only on whether f23f_{23} lies below or above the threshold value 5050. This is precisely the type of setting in which a decision aware estimator can differ sharply from a prediction-oriented one: not all directions of OD error are equally consequential, and errors that move the estimate across the decision boundary are much more important than errors that remain decision-neutral.

We set the true OD vector to f⋆=(35,49,65)⊤f^{\star}=(35,49,65)^{\top}, which satisfies the physical constraint f12+f13=100f_{12}+f_{13}=100. Under the true OD vector, min⁡{f23⋆,50}=min⁡{49,50}=49\min\{f_{23}^{\star},50\}=\min\{49,50\}=49, so the optimal solution is the f23f_{23}-driven action, i.e., w=(0,1,0)w=(0,1,0). We then construct a dataset of 300300 historical OD samples and consider the sample mean as the simplest benchmark predictor. To make the distinction between prediction error and decision impact transparent, we construct two subgroups of historical samples with comparable Euclidean deviation from the true OD vector but sharply different decision impacts:

  • •

    The first subgroup contains 200200 safe historical samples generated around the center f⋆+(10,0,−10)⊤f^{\star}+(10,0,-10)^{\top}. Specifically, for each sample we add an integer-valued perturbation (ε1,ε2,ε3)(\varepsilon_{1},\varepsilon_{2},\varepsilon_{3}), where ε1\varepsilon_{1} and ε3\varepsilon_{3} are constructed so that ε3=−ε1\varepsilon_{3}=-\varepsilon_{1}, and ε2\varepsilon_{2} is a relatively small perturbation around zero. These samples are intentionally displaced in a direction that mainly redistributes mass between f12f_{12} and f13f_{13} while leaving the decision-relevant component f23f_{23} nearly unchanged. As a result, although their mean squared deviation from the truth is non-negligible, their effect on the downstream decision is limited.

  • •

    The second subgroup contains 100100 risky historical samples generated around the center f⋆+(0,10​2,0)⊤f^{\star}+(0,10\sqrt{2},0)^{\top}, with moderate perturbations around that point. This group is constructed so that its Euclidean distance from the truth is of a similar magnitude to that of the safe group, but the displacement occurs primarily in the sensitive direction associated with f23f_{23}. Consequently, these samples are much more likely to move the estimate across the decision threshold and induce the wrong action.

This construction is deliberate. The safe and risky samples have nearly identical average Mean Squared Error (MSE) relative to the true OD vector—67.2767.27 for the safe group and 65.3565.35 for the risky group—and are therefore difficult to distinguish under a standard prediction metric. Yet their decision implications are very different. Most samples remain consistent with the correct downstream action, whereas a smaller subset is systematically shifted toward the wrong side of the decision boundary and thus behaves like decision-distorting outliers. These samples do not stand out in terms of MSE and do not dominate the dataset numerically, yet they are sufficient to shift a conventional predictor across the decision threshold and induce the wrong decision.

This distinction is reflected in both the aggregate prediction results and the geometry shown in Figure 3. Using the sample mean of the entire group of historical samples as a benchmark predictor, yields f^mean=(41.69, 53.62, 58.30)⊤\widehat{f}^{\mathrm{mean}}=(41.69,\;53.62,\;58.30)^{\top}. By contrast, the proposed Decision Aware Estimation (DWE) method returns f^DWE=(50.00, 49.90, 50.00)⊤\widehat{f}^{\mathrm{DWE}}=(50.00,\;49.90,\;50.00)^{\top}. In prediction terms, the sample mean is substantially closer to the ground truth: its MSE is 36.9636.96, whereas the DWE estimate has a much larger MSE of 150.27150.27. However, the performance reverses once decision quality is taken into account. Because f^23mean>50\widehat{f}_{23}^{\mathrm{mean}}>50, the sample mean induces the wrong decision; in contrast, because f^23DWE<50\widehat{f}_{23}^{\mathrm{DWE}}<50, the DWE estimate recovers the correct decision.

Figure 3 illustrates the example from two complementary perspectives. In the reduced 2-D view in panel (a), the downstream decision depends only on whether f23f_{23} lies above or below the threshold of 5050. Although most samples lie in the decision-consistent region, a small cluster of decision-distorting samples pulls the historical mean (blue point) across the boundary, despite its smaller MSE relative to the true OD vector (black star). The DWE solution (green triangle), in contrast, remains in the decision-consistent region. Panel (b) reveals the underlying geometry: the historical mean is pulled toward the center of the data cloud on the sensor-induced feasible manifold, improving data fidelity but crossing the projected decision boundary, whereas DWE optimizes the decision aware objective within the geometrically approximated feasible region and shifts the estimate toward a decision-robust region. Thus, lower prediction error does not necessarily translate into better operational performance.

Next, we examine a situation where historical samples violate the physical feasibility induced by hard data. We generate 300 historical OD samples:

  • •

    200200 regular samples satisfying the physical relation f12+f13=100f_{12}+f_{13}=100, with f12∈[25,45],f23∈[45,50],f13=100−f12.f_{12}\in[25,45],f_{23}\in[45,50],f_{13}=100-f_{12}.

  • •

    100100 infeasible samples for which f12f_{12} and f23f_{23} remain in the same range, but f13f_{13} is shifted downward so that f13=(100−f12)−ξ,ξ∈[20,30].f_{13}=(100-f_{12})-\xi,\xi\in[20,30]. As a result, these contaminated historical samples no longer lie on the physically feasible manifold.

This construction captures an important failure mode in OD learning: in practice, historical data may contain observations that are inconsistent with the current physical state of the network.

Figure 4 illustrates the effect of physically infeasible samples from two complementary perspectives. In the reduced 2-D view in panel (a), f12+f13=100f_{12}+f_{13}=100 defines the sensor-implied feasibility condition, while f23=(f12+f13)/2f_{23}=(f_{12}+f_{13})/2 defines the decision boundary. The infeasible samples (red points) pull the historical mean away from the physically feasible region, whereas DWE optimizes the decision aware objective directly over the feasible manifold, yielding a solution close to the true value while satisfying the physical constraints by construction. Panel (b) reveals the corresponding 3-D geometry: infeasible samples lie systematically off the manifold and distort the raw data cloud, making the historical mean an unreliable summary, while DWE remains anchored to the physically feasible region. Thus, physical constraints protect the estimator from sample errors that would otherwise pull it away from the structure of the current system.

This example illustrates the limitation of purely data-driven estimation. Historical observations are generated under heterogeneous network states, demand conditions, and behavioral responses, and thus populate a broad, high-dimensional space. However, once current observations and network conditions are imposed, the true OD vector is confined to a smaller feasible region lying on a smaller admissible manifold. A predictor may therefore fit the historical data well in a global sense and yet remain misaligned with the structure of the current system. This misalignment is both geometric and operational: some deviations are innocuous, while others are amplified through the downstream optimization, leading to substantial decision regret. The objective is not to reproduce historical patterns, but to extract an estimate that is physically grounded in current conditions and decision-relevant.

4.2 A Small Network for Benchmarking and Sensitivity Analysis

4.2.1 Network Configuration

Consider a network consisting of four terminal nodes connected through a single central junction, resulting in eight directed links. Each terminal node can serve as both an origin and a destination, yielding a total of 12 OD pairs. The network topology and link directions are illustrated in Figure 5. Let f∈ℝ+12f\in\mathbb{R}^{12}_{+} denote the OD flow vector and L∈ℝ+8L\in\mathbb{R}^{8}_{+} the corresponding link flow vector. The physical relationship between OD flows and link flows is encoded by a fixed link-OD incidence matrix X∈{0,1}8×12X\in\{0,1\}^{8\times 12}, such that L=X​fL=Xf.

4.2.2 Fabrication of True OD and Historical OD Samples

We use a polynomial function based on four features to generate historical OD samples and the true OD flows. The case P=1P=1 serves as the lowest-complexity benchmark, in which the latent OD index is linear in the features. Larger values of PP introduce increasing nonlinear structure in the feature-to-OD mapping. Specifically, for each polynomial order P∈{1,…,6}P\in\{1,\ldots,6\}, latent OD flows are generated from a polynomial transformation of the feature vector and then passed through a softplus transformation, Q=log⁡(1+exp⁡(Z))Q=\log(1+\exp(Z)), which guarantees non-negativity while preserving smoothness. Thus, varying PP creates OD samples with different levels of complexity and different degrees of model misspecification for linear prediction models. This allows us to evaluate how prediction-oriented and decision aware estimators perform as the historical OD data become increasingly nonlinear and harder to fit with a linear model.

For each value of PP, we generate separate training and testing samples. The training samples are used to construct prediction-oriented and decision aware OD estimators, while the testing samples are used to evaluate downstream decision quality. See Appendix H for details of the OD data-generation process.

4.2.3 Downstream Decision Problem

We use the demonstration investment allocation problem described in Appendix G as the downstream decision problem. This problem is formulated as a budget-constrained linear program, in which a transportation authority allocates a fixed investment budget across candidate road segments, and the resulting link improvements reduce OD-level travel times. For a given OD-flow estimate ff, the downstream problem returns an optimal investment allocation x∗​(f)x^{*}(f); the corresponding post-investment OD-level travel times are denoted by w∗​(f)w^{*}(f).

To avoid confounding the comparison with random variation from the downstream optimization problem, we evaluate all OD-estimation methods under the same investment environment within each experimental instance. Specifically, the OD-to-segment incidence matrix, baseline travel times, marginal improvement costs, and segment-level improvement upper bounds are generated once and then held fixed throughout the method comparison. The investment budget is also fixed and is set to 35%35\% of the maximum feasible investment level. Thus, the downstream LP is identical across methods except for the OD-flow vector used in the objective. This design ensures that differences in downstream performance are driven by the estimated OD vectors rather than by random variation in the underlying investment problem.

4.2.4 Benchmark Methods

We organize the benchmark methods according to two dimensions: the source of OD-demand information and the way this information is incorporated into the downstream decision problem. The first dimension distinguishes different forms of prior OD information available before solving the downstream optimization problem. In particular, we consider three historical-demand priors, denoted by ℛ={M,LR,Loc}\mathcal{R}=\{\mathrm{M},\mathrm{LR},\mathrm{Loc}\}. Here, M\mathrm{M} denotes the global historical mean, which uses the average OD vector over the historical sample. LR\mathrm{LR} denotes a model-based prediction obtained from a linear regression model trained to predict OD flows by minimizing mean squared error; this produces a single point estimate for the current instance. Loc\mathrm{Loc} denotes a local historical-demand prior, which uses multiple historical OD samples associated with covariate values similar to the current instance. In our implementation, this local prior is constructed by averaging the OD vectors of the kk-nearest historical samples in the covariate space.11 1 More generally, this prior can be viewed as a local regression estimate, and other nonparametric regression methods beyond kk-nearest neighbors can also be used; see Appendix B and Bertsimas and Kallus (2020).

We first evaluate these priors under a standard predict-then-optimize (PTO) pipeline. In this class of methods, an OD vector is first estimated without using the downstream decision objective, and the resulting point estimate is then passed directly to the investment allocation problem. This gives three PTO baselines: PTO-M,PTO-LR,PTO-Loc\textsc{PTO-M},\textsc{PTO-LR},\textsc{PTO-Loc}, corresponding respectively to the global historical mean, the linear-regression prediction, and the local historical-demand prior. These baselines represent the conventional sequential approach in which OD estimation quality and downstream decision quality are optimized separately.

In addition to these demand-side priors, we include an OLS benchmark based on observed link-flow information. This method reconstructs OD flows from observed link flows through a least-squares formulation and then applies the downstream investment model to the reconstructed OD vector. The OLS benchmark therefore represents the information available from the link-flow observation side, in contrast to the historical-demand priors used by the PTO baselines.

We then compare these baselines with two direct-reformulation DWE methods. For each prior-information source r∈{M,LR,Loc}r\in\{\mathrm{M},\mathrm{LR},\mathrm{Loc}\}, we denote the DWE-original and DWE-Ellipsoid formulations introduced in Section 3.4 by D-Full-​r\textsc{D-Full-}r and D-Geo-​r\textsc{D-Geo-}r, respectively. The former optimizes the SPO+ surrogate over the original link-flow consistent OD feasible region, whereas the latter uses its ellipsoidal approximation. This paired comparison isolates the effect of the feasible-region approximation while holding the prior-information source and decision aware loss fixed.

4.2.5 Regret Behavior under Increasing Demand Generation Nonlinearity

This experiment examines how downstream decision regret changes as the polynomial order increases from 1 to 6, thereby introducing progressively stronger nonlinearity into the true demand generation process. This setting allows us to evaluate whether each method remains decision reliable as the actual demand generation mechanism becomes more complex and prediction-centered estimators are increasingly exposed to model misspecification. The comparison is motivated by a central curiosity: Whether and how does model misspecification translate prediction errors into unreliable downstream decisions? Specifically, we will answer three empirical questions. First, does increasing demand-generation nonlinearity undermine the downstream reliability of decisions produced by prediction-centered methods? Second, conditional on using the same historical demand information, does decision aware estimation provide additional regret reduction beyond standard PTO? Third, are these gains concentrated in average performance, or do they also translate into lower upper-tail regret and greater stability across training samples?

Figure 6 summarizes the effect of model misspecification (indicated by increasing demand generation nonlinearity) on downstream decision quality. We first consider Panel (a), which reports the average test-set regret. The OLS benchmark provides a useful contrast because it relies only on observed link-flow consistency and does not use any historical OD-demand prior. Its regret varies substantially across polynomial orders. This behavior reflects the ill-posed nature of OD reconstruction merely from aggregate link flows: many OD vectors can be consistent with the same link-flow observations, but they may induce very different investment decisions, thus leading to unstable downstream regret.

Among the PTO baselines, PTO-M performs poorly because it relies only on a coarse global mean prior and ignores the covariate information of the current instance. Incorporating covariate information substantially improves performance in the low-order regime, reflected by the low regrets produced by PTO-LR and PTO-Loc. For example, PTO-LR produced 4.174.17 at order 1, which reflects the advantage of the linear predictor when the true demand-generation process is close to the assumed model class. However, as the polynomial order increases and model misspecification becomes more severe, both PTO-LR and PTO-Loc deteriorate rapidly.

We next compare the DWE methods in Panel (a). The D-Full-​r\textsc{D-Full-}r methods provide clear improvements over their PTO counterparts at low and intermediate orders, confirming the value of incorporating downstream decision structure into the OD-estimation step. However, their performance becomes less stable in the high-order regime. For instance, at order 6, regret remains at 284.11284.11 for D-Full-M, 226.08226.08 for D-Full-LR, and 224.47224.47 for D-Full-Loc. In contrast, the D-Geo-​r\textsc{D-Geo-}r methods form the most stable group across orders and prior sources. At order 6, D-Geo-LR and D-Geo-Loc achieve regrets of 79.8079.80 and 73.7673.76, respectively. The gap between D-Full-​r\textsc{D-Full-}r and D-Geo-​r\textsc{D-Geo-}r is particularly informative. Since both methods use the same decision aware objective, their difference is driven primarily by the feasible-region representation. The superior stability of D-Geo-​r\textsc{D-Geo-}r suggests that the geometric approximation plays a role similar to regularization: it constrains the OD estimate to a more stable and decision-relevant region, thereby preventing the direct decision aware fit over the full feasible set from becoming overly sensitive in high-complexity settings.

Panels (b) and (c) further show that the main benefit of the regularized DWE methods is not limited to the average regret. Panel (b) reports the 80th percentile test-set regret. At this level, differences among the stronger methods become much smaller. In particular, the D-Geo-​r\textsc{D-Geo-}r methods attain values that are essentially zero across nearly all orders and prior sources, indicating that they incur little or no regret for a large majority of test instances. Thus, much of the average-regret difference in Panel (a) is not driven by the bulk of ordinary test cases, but rather by a smaller set of more difficult instances. This interpretation is confirmed by Panel (c), where the 90th percentile regret reveals much sharper separation across methods. Once attention shifts to the upper tail of the regret distribution, the risk-control advantage of the regularized DWE methods becomes clear. For example, at order 6 under the local prior, the 90th percentile regret is 336.17336.17 for PTO-Loc, 173.13173.13 for D-Full-Loc, and 37.5337.53 for D-Geo-Loc. Under the linear-regression prior at the same order, the corresponding values are 634.22634.22 for PTO-LR, 194.11194.11 for D-Full-LR, and 55.7355.73 for D-Geo-LR. Therefore, the main advantage of the D-Geo-​r\textsc{D-Geo-}r methods lies not only in reducing average regret, but also in suppressing rare but severe decision failures. This type of tail robustness becomes increasingly important as the true demand-generation mechanism grows more nonlinear.

Figure 7 complements the heatmap by showing the within-prior distribution of mean test-set regret across training seeds. This figure addresses whether the improvement of the DWE methods is driven by a few favorable training samples or is systematic across training realizations. In the high-order regimes, PTO-LR and PTO-Loc have not only higher median regret, but also wider boxes, longer upper whiskers, and more extreme outliers. This indicates that, under stronger nonlinearity, PTO becomes highly sensitive to the particular training sample: some seeds lead to especially poor downstream decisions. In contrast, the D-Geo variants shift the entire seed-level distribution downward and keep it substantially more concentrated. Thus, their improvement is not driven by a small number of favorable training seeds. Rather, they systematically reduce variability and suppress high-regret training realizations.

Finally, Figure 8 decomposes the reduction in regret into three incremental sources. The first is the gain from using a covariate-aligned historical prior. Moving from PTO-M to PTO-Loc lowers regret across all polynomial orders, indicating that matching historical OD information to the current covariate realization is valuable. However, this improvement alone is not sufficient: in the nonlinear regime, PTO-Loc still exhibits substantial regret. The second gain comes from adding the decision aware objective and physical OD constraints. Relative to PTO-Loc, D-Full-Loc further reduces regret, showing that decision aware refinement provides value beyond prediction-centered use of the same prior. The third and largest high-order gain comes from the geometric approximation. Compared with the full-constraint decision aware estimator, D-Geo-Loc achieves a much lower regret in the nonlinear regime, suggesting that restricting the update to a stable, decision-relevant region is crucial.

Overall, the results provide consistent answers to the three empirical questions posed above. First, increasing level of model misspecification (indicated by demand-generation nonlinearity) does undermine the downstream reliability of prediction-centered methods. Although historical priors that exploit current-instance covariate information improve substantially upon a crude global mean, PTO methods still deteriorate markedly in the highly nonlinear regime. Second, conditional on using the same historical demand information, decision aware estimation provides additional regret reduction beyond standard PTO, showing that downstream decision structure contains useful information for OD estimation. However, direct decision aware fitting over the full feasible set can remain unstable when the demand-generation process becomes sufficiently complex. Third, the benefits of introducing the geometric approximation in the decision aware estimation problem yields clear benefits, reducing both the average and upper-tail regret across training samples.

4.2.6 Robustness to Noisy Historical OD Labels

The previous experiments varied the structural complexity of the OD generation process. We next examine a complementary source of misspecification: noisy historical OD labels. The central question is: holding the data-generating process fixed, how sensitive are prediction centered and decision centered estimators to increasing noise in the historical OD information used to construct their priors?

Figure 9 reports the resulting regret sensitivity. In this experiment, we fix the polynomial order at three and add independent nonnegative uniform perturbations to the historical OD demand. The perturbation magnitude increases with the noise level, and the noisy OD entries are clipped to remain within the feasible demand range. The test set and the underlying data-generating process are held fixed, so the experiment isolates the effect of corrupted historical outcome information on downstream decision quality. Since the OLS benchmark is not affected by this historical-label perturbation, we use it as the normalization baseline and report

Reduction vs. OLS=100⋅RegretOLS−RegretmRegretOLS.\text{Reduction vs. OLS}=100\cdot\frac{\text{Regret}_{\mathrm{OLS}}-\text{Regret}_{m}}{\text{Regret}_{\mathrm{OLS}}}.

The global mean historical prior is omitted because its performance is uniformly poor, allowing the comparison to focus on the LR\mathrm{LR} and Loc\mathrm{Loc}. Under both prior constructions, the PTO methods deteriorate as the historical OD labels become noisier. Both PTO-LR and PTO-Loc initially achieve substantial regret reductions relative to OLS, but their advantages vanish and eventually become negative as the noise level increases. The two PTO variants, however, exhibit different deterioration patterns. PTO-Loc declines more quickly and more smoothly, indicating that the local prior is immediately affected by noisy neighboring historical observations. PTO-LR is more stable at moderate noise levels, but after the perturbation exceeds a critical range, its regret reduction drops sharply and falls below the OLS baseline. This behavior indicates that PTO is highly sensitive to corrupted historical labels, because the downstream optimization is driven by a single predictive reference that becomes increasingly unreliable.

The decision aware estimator with the full structural constraints also becomes less stable under noise. In both panels, D-FULL starts with a sizable reduction relative to OLS but declines sharply as the perturbation level increases. Nevertheless, it continues to improve upon the corresponding PTO baseline over most of the noise range. This suggests that incorporating the decision objective remains beneficial, but an unrestricted decision aware fit can overreact to noisy historical signals. By contrast, the ellipsoidal approximation is substantially more robust. The D-Geo-​r\textsc{D-Geo-}r methods maintain a large and nearly flat regret reduction across the entire noise range in both the LR\mathrm{LR} and Loc\mathrm{Loc} panels. Although their performance also decreases mildly as noise increases, the decline is much smaller than that of PTO or D-FULL. This stability suggests that the ellipsoidal restriction filters out noisy directions in the historical OD information while preserving the decision-relevant region of the feasible set.

Overall, this experiment reinforces the main robustness message of the paper. Historical OD information is useful only if it is incorporated in a way that is stable under label corruption. Methods that prioritize data alignment alone quickly lose their downstream advantage as historical labels become noisy, whereas decision aware methods with geometric regularization remain robust, preserving meaningful regret reductions even under high noise.

4.2.7 Sensitivity of the Tuning Parameter α\alpha to Label Noise

We next examine how sensitive the decision aware estimator is to the SPO+ surrogate parameter α\alpha when the historical OD prior are noisy. Following the same noisy setting as above, we perturb the historical OD samples used to construct the local prior and evaluate the test-set decision regret of D-Geo-Loc over a grid of positive α\alpha values. For each noise level η\eta, let Rη​(α)R_{\eta}(\alpha) denote the average test-set regret obtained using tuning parameter α\alpha. To measure sensitivity relative to the best value in the grid, we define the excess-regret sensitivity function

Sη​(α)=Rη​(α)−minα′∈𝒜⁡Rη​(α′),S_{\eta}(\alpha)=R_{\eta}(\alpha)-\min_{\alpha^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}R_{\eta}(\alpha^{\prime}),

where 𝒜\mathcal{A} is the set of positive α\alpha values considered in the experiment. A smaller value of Sη​(α)S_{\eta}(\alpha) indicates that the performance at α\alpha is close to the best achievable performance for that noise level.

Figure 10 reports the sensitivity of D-Geo-Loc to the tuning parameter α\alpha under different levels of label noise. The left panel shows a clear decreasing pattern in average regret as α\alpha moves away from very small values. When α=0.1\alpha=0.1 or 0.50.5, the regret remains relatively high across all noise levels, indicating that too small a value of α\alpha provides insufficient decision guidance. As α\alpha increases to a moderate range, especially around α=2\alpha=2, the regret drops substantially and then becomes relatively flat for larger values. This empirical pattern is broadly consistent with the standard SPO+ formulation, where α=2\alpha=2 is the canonical scaling used in the Fisher-consistency analysis of the SPO+ surrogate (Elmachtoub and Grigas 2022). The right panel reports the excess-regret sensitivity function Sη​(α)S_{\eta}(\alpha). Consistent with the left panel, small values of α\alpha incur a noticeable excess regret, while moderate and large values produce performance close to the best value within each noise level. This suggests that DWE does not require fine tuning of α\alpha under mild to moderate label noise, which is practically useful because the method does not depend on a highly delicate hyperparameter choice. Rather, the main requirement is to avoid overly small values of α\alpha; once α\alpha is sufficiently positive, the estimator achieves relatively stable decision performance across the noise levels considered.

4.3 Sioux Falls network

We further evaluate the proposed decision aware estimation framework on a larger and more realistic transportation network, the Sioux Falls network. This network consists of 24 nodes, 76 directed links, and 552 OD pairs. The physical relationship between OD flows and link flows is encoded by a fixed link-OD incidence matrix X∈ℝ76×552X\in\mathbb{R}^{76\times 552} in L=X​fL=Xf, leading to a substantially higher-dimensional and more severely underdetermined estimation problem than the synthetic intersection network considered earlier.

4.3.1 OD Demand Patterns

To assess robustness across heterogeneous demand structures, we construct five distinct OD demand patterns on the Sioux Falls network. These patterns are designed to capture qualitatively different spatial and structural characteristics commonly observed in real transportation systems: distance decay, hub-spoke concentration, community block structure, directional corridors, and low-rank latent demand. Figure 11 illustrates the resulting OD matrices together with their induced link-flow patterns. While these demand modes exhibit markedly different spatial organizations, all satisfy the same physical flow conservation constraints. Detailed descriptions of the demand construction and their statistical properties are provided in Appendix I.1.

4.3.2 Experimental Design

For all five demand patterns, we generate OD-flow priors using a gravity model with imperfect features, providing a common prior across all experiments. We consider three total-demand levels: low (1,0001{,}000), medium (10,00010{,}000), and high (20,00020{,}000).

We compare OLS, PTO, and two DWE variants. OLS reconstructs OD flows from observed link flows using least squares, while PTO directly optimizes the downstream problem using the gravity-model prediction. Following the previous name convention, DWE methods are denoted by D-Full-G\mathrm{G} and D-Geo-G\mathrm{G}, where G\mathrm{G} denotes the gravity-model prior. D-Full-G directly solves the full decision aware estimation formulation, whereas D-Geo-G uses the proposed geometry-based formulation; for D-Geo-G, we evaluate multiple radii and report the best-performing radius r∗r^{*}.

Table 1 summarizes the performances across all demand patterns and demand levels, evaluated using downstream decision regret.

4.3.3 Results

Table 1 documents a clear advantage of decision aware estimation on the Sioux Falls network. OLS yields the largest decision regret in all 15 demand-level–mode combinations, highlighting the limitations of recovering OD demand from link-flow consistency alone in a severely underdetermined system. PTO substantially improves upon OLS by incorporating the gravity-model prediction, but considerable decision regret remains in several settings. Both DWE variants deliver further gains: D-Full-G achieves strictly lower decision regret than PTO in 10 of the 15 cases and matches it in the remaining five, while D-Geo-G improves upon PTO in 11 cases and matches it in the other four. Among the cases with strict improvement, the reduction relative to PTO ranges from 52.2%52.2\% to 100%100\% for D-Full-G and from 68.7%68.7\% to 100%100\% for D-Geo-G. Across all 15 cases, the simple average regret decreases from 184.00184.00 under PTO to 64.4064.40 under D-Full-G and 38.1938.19 under D-Geo-G, corresponding to reductions of approximately 65.0%65.0\% and 79.2%79.2\%, respectively. To assess whether these conclusions are robust to variation across experimental realizations, we conduct an additional repeated-sampling experiment reported in Appendix Table 3. Each setting is repeated 20 times, and the mean decision regret is reported. D-Full-G and D-Geo-G strictly outperform PTO and OLS in all 15 settings, confirming the robustness of decision aware estimation. Thus, explicitly accounting for the downstream decision produces substantial improvements without deteriorating decision quality in any of the baseline scenarios. A direct comparison of the two DWE variants provides evidence of an additional regularization effect from the geometric formulation. For D-Geo-G, Table 1 reports the best result over the tested radii. D-Geo-G achieves decision regret that is lower than or equal to that of D-Full-G in all 15 cases: it performs strictly better in five cases and matches D-Full-G in the remaining ten. Its average regret is also 40.7%40.7\% lower than that of D-Full-G (38.1938.19 versus 64.4064.40).

One may notice that the magnitude of decision regrets varies sharply across demand patterns. It would be interesting to explore how demand-prediction error propagates through downstream problems of different network structures, but it is beyond the scope of this work.

On the other hand, the gain of D-Geo-G in performance robustness comes at a substantial computational cost. As shown in Figure 12, D-Full-G solves in 0.9220.922 seconds on average, with a median of 0.9210.921 seconds and a standard deviation of only 0.0110.011 seconds. D-Geo-G, by contrast, requires 19.45519.455 seconds on average, with a median of 17.84517.845 seconds and a standard deviation of 5.8355.835 seconds.
