Thus, D-Geo-G requires approximately 21.121.1 times the mean solve time of D-Full-G. The runtime of D-Full-G across all instances is similar, while D-Geo-G‘s runtime seem to vary by instances. D-Full-G is therefore preferable when computational efficiency is paramount, while D-Geo-G offers a more conservative alternative when the additional protection against over-adaptation justifies the computational premium.

5 Conclusions and Future Research

As we conclude this study, we reflect on a broader lesson that extends beyond OD estimation. OD demand is not directly observed and must instead be inferred from indirect information, such as observed link flows, physical network constraints, and prior demand patterns. These sources help characterize which OD estimates are plausible, but plausibility alone does not determine which estimate is most useful. A key premise we emphasize is: not all estimation errors are consequential in the same way. A good estimate should be faithful enough to the world we observe, but attentive to the consequences of the decisions it informs. Through analytical and numerical results, we have shown that accounting for how estimates are ultimately used can substantially improve their value for downstream decision-making.

Beyond knowledge from transportation science, our research design draws on two complementary methodological perspectives: geometry and stochastic optimization. A geometric perspective shapes how we view and represent the demand space. OD demand vectors are typically modeled in a high-dimensional space whose dimension equals the number of OD pairs in the network. A central message from this study is that a realistic OD demand does not occupy the entire ambient space. Instead, it is implicitly restricted by a variety of physical and behavioral constraints. These structural restrictions imply that feasible OD demand vectors lie on a much lower-dimensional manifold embedded in the high-dimensional OD space. Ignoring this geometric structure can lead to misleading conclusions in data-driven prediction. A stochastic optimization perspective provides a flexible framework for integrating data, prior knowledge, physical constraints, and decision regret within a unified model. Equally important, advances in stochastic optimization provide the theoretical and computational tools needed to solve the resulting models efficiently and reliably. Our experience with these complementary perspectives also points to a broader lesson: new research challenges often benefit from ideas that lie outside the traditional boundaries of a discipline. Particularly for young scholars, the broader the set of intellectual building blocks one acquires, the better prepared one may be to construct solutions to challenges not yet anticipated.

The present study opens several promising directions for future research, spanning modeling generality, data reliability, theoretical analysis, and algorithmic development. First and foremost, while the linear constraints considered in this study capture fundamental flow conservation laws, real transportation systems are governed by richer physical mechanisms, including nonlinear constraints and dynamic relations that may be expressed through differential or difference equations. Accommodating such general physical constraints would substantially broaden its applicability, while also posing new analytical and computational challenges. Second, the reliability of link-flow observations themselves deserves explicit attention. In this paper, link flows are treated as accurate measurements that define a consistent constraint system. Developing principled methods to handle imperfect link-flow observations, such as through soft constraints, feasibility robust formulations, or joint estimation of OD flows and link-flow errors, remains an important and challenging direction for future research. In additional, a natural extension is to consider more complex decision problems, including those with nonlinear objectives, integer decisions, equilibrium constraints, or multistage structures. Such extensions would allow the framework to capture a broader class of transportation decisions, but would also require new tools to analyze regret, tractability, and solution stability. Finally, how to characterize regret presents future research opportunities. For example, while the current results provide initial bounds, sharper regret guarantees—such as tighter upper bounds, lower bounds, or instance-dependent characterizations—are needed to better understand the fundamental limits of decision aware OD estimation. These directions are not simply extensions of the present framework; they point toward a broader opportunity to rethink how estimation and decision-making should interact. As increasingly rich data and increasingly consequential decisions become intertwined, we believe that learning not only from the data, but also from how the data will ultimately be used, offers a promising path forward.

Appendix A Ellipsoidal Radius and Calibration

Let d=dim(ker⁡X)=n−qd=\dim(\ker X)=n-q and consider the ellipsoidal search region ℬH​(r)={u∈ℝd|u⊤​H​u≤r2}\mathcal{B}_{H}(r)=\left\{u\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\;\middle|\;u^{\top}Hu\leq r^{2}\right\}, where H≻0H\succ 0 is the Hessian of the logarithmic barrier evaluated at the analytic-center. Let H=Q​Λ​Q⊤H=Q\Lambda Q^{\top}, Λ=diag⁡(λ1,…,λd)\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{d}). Under the coordinate transformation y=Q⊤​uy=Q^{\top}u, the ellipsoid becomes ∑i=1dλi​yi2≤r2\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda_{i}y_{i}^{2}\leq r^{2}, or equivalently ∑i=1dyi2/(r2/λi)≤1\sum_{i=1}^{d}y_{i}^{2}/(r^{2}/\lambda_{i})\leq 1. Comparing this with the standard ellipsoid form ∑i=1dyi2/ai2≤1\sum_{i=1}^{d}y_{i}^{2}/a_{i}^{2}\leq 1, the principal semiaxis along the iith eigenvector of HH is ai​(r)=r/λia_{i}(r)=r/\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}. Thus, rr controls the overall scale of the ellipsoid, while the eigenvalues λi\lambda_{i} determine its relative shape across directions. Increasing rr by a factor α\alpha expands every principal semiaxis by the same factor α\alpha.

The effect of dimension can also be seen from the volume of the ellipsoid. Its dd-dimensional volume is

Vold⁡(ℬH​(r))=πd/2Γ⁡(d/2+1)​rddetH.\operatorname{Vol}_{d}\bigl(\mathcal{B}_{H}(r)\bigr)=\frac{\pi^{d/2}}{\Gamma(d/2+1)}\frac{r^{d}}{\sqrt{\det H}}.

Defining gH=(detH)1/dg_{H}=(\det H)^{1/d}, and applying Stirling’s approximation gives

Vold⁡(ℬH​(r))∼1π​d​(2​π​e​r2d​gH)d/2.\operatorname{Vol}_{d}\bigl(\mathcal{B}_{H}(r)\bigr)\sim\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi d}}\left(\frac{2\pi e\,r^{2}}{d\,g_{H}}\right)^{d/2}.

Therefore, under a fixed coordinate normalization, the volume represented by a fixed radius rr can change substantially with the nullspace dimension dd. For example, when H=IH=I and r=1r=1, the ellipsoid reduces to the Euclidean unit ball. Its volume decreases from approximately 2.552.55 in 1010 dimensions to 2.58×10−22.58\times 10^{-2} in 2020 dimensions, and further to 1.73×10−131.73\times 10^{-13} in 5050 dimensions. Thus, the same numerical value of rr can correspond to very different volumetric coverage as the dimension of the nullspace changes.

This observation suggests a simple heuristic for choosing the radius as the dimension changes. From the leading term in the volume approximation, the quantity r2d​gH\frac{r^{2}}{d\,g_{H}} determines the exponential scale of the ellipsoid volume, suggesting the scaling r∝d​gHr\propto\sqrt{d\,g_{H}}. We first select a representative reference instance and choose r0r_{0} from a set of candidate radii by minimizing the downstream regret on a validation set. Let d0d_{0} and H0H_{0} denote the nullspace dimension and Hessian of this reference instance, and let gH,0=(detH0)1/d0g_{H,0}=(\det H_{0})^{1/d_{0}} denote the corresponding Hessian geometric mean. We scale the validated radius r0r_{0} to a new instance according to

rheur=max⁡{1,r0​d​gHd0​gH,0}.r_{\mathrm{heur}}=\max\left\{1,\;r_{0}\sqrt{\frac{d\,g_{H}}{d_{0}\,g_{H,0}}}\right\}.

For example, if gH≈gH,0g_{H}\approx g_{H,0} and validation selects r0=1r_{0}=1 for a reference instance with d0=10d_{0}=10, the rule gives approximately rheur=2r_{\mathrm{heur}}=2 for d=40d=40 and rheur=3r_{\mathrm{heur}}=3 for d=90d=90. In this case, the rule reduces to r∝dr\propto\sqrt{d}. The heuristic transfers the radius calibrated on the reference instance to problems with different dimensions and Hessian geometries, and the resulting value can be further refined using validation data if needed.

Appendix B Construction of the Local Error Distribution

This appendix describes how the error distribution 𝒫\mathcal{P} can be constructed from historical data and contextual information. Let 𝒟={(xd,rd)}d=1D\mathcal{D}=\{(x_{d},r_{d})\}_{d=1}^{D} denote a historical dataset, where xdx_{d} contains contextual information associated with observation dd, such as historical demand, socioeconomic characteristics, land use, and other factors related to travel demand. The residual rdr_{d} measures the error of the prior OD estimate for that observation. In particular, if f0,df_{0,d} denotes the prior estimate and fdobsf_{d}^{\mathrm{obs}} the corresponding historical OD observation, we define rd=fdobs−f0,dr_{d}=f_{d}^{\mathrm{obs}}-f_{0,d}.

For a target instance with contextual features x⋆x^{\star}, we use historical observations with similar features to characterize the uncertainty in the prior estimate f0f_{0}. Following the local weighting perspective of Bertsimas and Kallus (2020), we define a neighborhood 𝒩⁡(x⋆)⊆{1,…,D}\mathcal{N}(x^{\star})\subseteq\{1,\ldots,D\} that determines which historical residuals contribute to the local error distribution. A simple empirical construction is

𝒫^​(x⋆)=1|𝒩⁡(x⋆)|​∑d∈𝒩⁡(x⋆)δrd,\widehat{\mathcal{P}}(x^{\star})=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}(x^{\star})|}\sum_{d\in\mathcal{N}(x^{\star})}\delta_{r_{d}},

where δrd\delta_{r_{d}} denotes a point mass at residual rdr_{d}. Different methods for defining 𝒩⁡(x⋆)\mathcal{N}(x^{\star}) correspond to different notions of similarity in the feature space. We consider several standard constructions below.

B.1 kk-nearest neighbors (kNN)

The kk-nearest-neighbor neighborhood consists of the kk historical observations whose feature vectors are closest to x⋆x^{\star} under a chosen distance metric d​i​s​(⋅,⋅)dis(\cdot,\cdot):

𝒩kNN​(x⋆)={d:xd​ is among the ​k​ closest points to ​x⋆​ under ​d​i​s​(⋅,⋅)}.\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{kNN}}(x^{\star})=\left\{d:x_{d}\text{ is among the }k\text{ closest points to }x^{\star}\text{ under }dis(\cdot,\cdot)\right\}. (12)

This construction fixes the number of residual observations used to estimate the local error distribution.

B.2 ε\varepsilon-ball neighborhood

An ε\varepsilon-ball neighborhood includes all historical observations within distance ε\varepsilon of x⋆x^{\star}:

𝒩ε​(x⋆)={d:‖xd−x⋆‖≤ε}.\mathcal{N}_{\varepsilon}(x^{\star})=\left\{d:\|x_{d}-x^{\star}\|\leq\varepsilon\right\}. (13)

The resulting neighborhood size adapts to the local density of the feature space.

B.3 Decision tree-based neighborhood

A decision tree trained on the historical data partitions the feature space into axis-aligned regions. The neighborhood contains observations that fall in the same terminal leaf as x⋆x^{\star}:

𝒩tree​(x⋆)={d:xd​ and ​x⋆​ lie in the same terminal leaf}.\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{tree}}(x^{\star})=\left\{d:x_{d}\text{ and }x^{\star}\text{ lie in the same terminal leaf}\right\}. (14)

This construction allows the neighborhood to reflect feature relevance and interactions learned from the historical data.

B.4 Kernel-based neighborhood

A kernel-based construction assigns each historical residual a weight

wd=K⁡(‖xd−x⋆‖h),w_{d}=K\!\left(\frac{\|x_{d}-x^{\star}\|}{h}\right), (15)

where K⁡(⋅)K(\cdot) is a kernel function and hh is a bandwidth parameter. After normalization, w~d=wd/∑j=1Dwj\tilde{w}_{d}=w_{d}/\sum_{j=1}^{D}w_{j}, the local error distribution can be written as

𝒫^​(x⋆)=∑d=1Dw~d​δrd.\widehat{\mathcal{P}}(x^{\star})=\sum_{d=1}^{D}\tilde{w}_{d}\,\delta_{r_{d}}.

This weighted construction avoids a discrete neighborhood boundary and gives greater influence to historical observations that are more similar to the target instance.

Appendix C Proof of Proposition 3.1

We prove the three stated properties of ℓα\ell_{\alpha} for any realized OD-flow vector f∗f^{\ast}, candidate OD estimate ff, and α>0\alpha>0.

Proof C.1

Proof. We begin by recalling the definition of regret. For a given decision rule w⁡(f)w(f), the regret associated with a realized OD flow f∗f^{\ast} is

R⁡(f∗,f)=f∗⊤​w​(f)−c⁡(f∗),R(f^{\ast},f)={f^{\ast}}^{\!\top}w(f)-c(f^{\ast}),

where c⁡(f∗):=minw∈𝒲⁡f∗⊤​w=f∗⊤​w​(f∗)c(f^{\ast}):=\min_{w\in\mathcal{W}}{f^{\ast}}^{\!\top}w={f^{\ast}}^{\!\top}w(f^{\ast}) and w⁡(f)∈arg⁡minw∈𝒲​f⊤​ww(f)\in\arg\min_{w\in\mathcal{W}}f^{\top}w denotes an optimal solution to the downstream optimization problem under ff.

Step 1 (Upper bound). Fix any α>0\alpha>0. Using f⊤​w​(f)=c⁡(f)f^{\top}w(f)=c(f), we have

R⁡(f∗,f)\displaystyle R(f^{\ast},f) =f∗⊤​w​(f)−c⁡(f∗)\displaystyle={f^{\ast}}^{\!\top}w(f)-c(f^{\ast})
=(f∗−α​f)⊤​w​(f)+α​c​(f)−c⁡(f∗)\displaystyle=(f^{\ast}-\alpha f)^{\top}w(f)+\alpha c(f)-c(f^{\ast})
≤maxw∈𝒲⁡(f∗−α​f)⊤​w+α​c​(f)−c⁡(f∗).\displaystyle\leq\max_{w\in\mathcal{W}}(f^{\ast}-\alpha f)^{\top}w+\alpha c(f)-c(f^{\ast}).

Since w⁡(f∗)∈𝒲w(f^{\ast})\in\mathcal{W} is feasible for the downstream problem under ff,

c⁡(f)=f⊤​w​(f)≤f⊤​w​(f∗).c(f)=f^{\top}w(f)\leq f^{\top}w(f^{\ast}).

Because α>0\alpha>0, it follows that

R⁡(f∗,f)\displaystyle R(f^{\ast},f) ≤maxw∈𝒲⁡(f∗−α​f)⊤​w+α​f⊤​w​(f∗)−c⁡(f∗)\displaystyle\leq\max_{w\in\mathcal{W}}(f^{\ast}-\alpha f)^{\top}w+\alpha f^{\top}w(f^{\ast})-c(f^{\ast})
=ℓα​(f∗,f).\displaystyle=\ell_{\alpha}(f^{\ast},f).

Hence,

R⁡(f∗,f)≤ℓα​(f∗,f),R(f^{\ast},f)\leq\ell_{\alpha}(f^{\ast},f),

which proves the first property in Proposition 3.1.

Step 2 (Convexity). For fixed f∗f^{\ast}, the surrogate can be written as

ℓα​(f∗,f)=maxw∈𝒲⁡{(f∗−α​f)⊤​w+α​f⊤​w​(f∗)−c⁡(f∗)}.\ell_{\alpha}(f^{\ast},f)=\max_{w\in\mathcal{W}}\left\{(f^{\ast}-\alpha f)^{\top}w+\alpha f^{\top}w(f^{\ast})-c(f^{\ast})\right\}.

For each fixed w∈𝒲w\in\mathcal{W}, the expression inside the maximum is affine, and hence convex, in ff. Therefore, by the supremum rule for convex functions (Royset and Wets 2021, Proposition 1.18(a)), ℓα​(f∗,⋅)\ell_{\alpha}(f^{\ast},\cdot) is convex. This proves the second property in Proposition 3.1.

Step 3 (Subgradient characterization).

For fixed f∗f^{\ast} and each w∈𝒲w\in\mathcal{W}, the expression inside the maximum in (7) is affine in ff, with gradient α⁡(w⁡(f∗)−w)\alpha\bigl(w(f^{\ast})-w\bigr). Since 𝒲\mathcal{W} is compact, Proposition 6.30 of Royset and Wets (2021) implies

∂fℓα​(f∗,f)=con⁡{α⁡(w⁡(f∗)−w):w∈arg⁡maxw~∈𝒲​(f∗−α​f)⊤​w~},\partial_{f}\ell_{\alpha}(f^{\ast},f)=\operatorname{con}\left\{\alpha\bigl(w(f^{\ast})-w\bigr):w\in\arg\max_{\tilde{w}\in\mathcal{W}}(f^{\ast}-\alpha f)^{\top}\tilde{w}\right\},

where con⁡(⋅)\operatorname{con}(\cdot) denotes the convex hull. Moreover,

arg⁡maxw∈𝒲​(f∗−α​f)⊤​w=arg⁡minw∈𝒲​(α​f−f∗)⊤​w.\arg\max_{w\in\mathcal{W}}(f^{\ast}-\alpha f)^{\top}w=\arg\min_{w\in\mathcal{W}}(\alpha f-f^{\ast})^{\top}w.

Therefore, choosing w⁡(α​f−f∗)w(\alpha f-f^{\ast}) from this optimal set yields

α⁡(w⁡(f∗)−w⁡(α​f−f∗))∈∂fℓα​(f∗,f),\alpha\bigl(w(f^{\ast})-w(\alpha f-f^{\ast})\bigr)\in\partial_{f}\ell_{\alpha}(f^{\ast},f),

which proves the third property in Proposition 3.1. □\square

Appendix D Proof of Proposition 3.2

Proof D.1

Proof.

We first decompose the discrepancy between the surrogate evaluated at the realized OD flow f∗f^{\ast} and the regret under the true OD flow ftruef_{\rm true} as

ℓα​(f∗,f)−R⁡(ftrue,f)=[ℓα​(ftrue,f)−R⁡(ftrue,f)]+[ℓα​(f∗,f)−ℓα​(ftrue,f)].\ell_{\alpha}(f^{\ast},f)-R(f_{\rm true},f)=\bigl[\ell_{\alpha}(f_{\rm true},f)-R(f_{\rm true},f)\bigr]+\bigl[\ell_{\alpha}(f^{\ast},f)-\ell_{\alpha}(f_{\rm true},f)\bigr].

We bound these two terms separately.

Step 1 (Surrogate approximation). From the definitions of ℓα\ell_{\alpha} and RR, we have

ℓα​(ftrue,f)−R⁡(ftrue,f)=\displaystyle\ell_{\alpha}(f_{\rm true},f)-R(f_{\rm true},f)={} maxw∈𝒲⁡(ftrue−α​f)⊤​(w−w⁡(f))+α​f⊤​(w⁡(ftrue)−w⁡(f)).\displaystyle\max_{w\in\mathcal{W}}(f_{\rm true}-\alpha f)^{\top}\bigl(w-w(f)\bigr)+\alpha f^{\top}\bigl(w(f_{\rm true})-w(f)\bigr).

For any w∈𝒲w\in\mathcal{W}, the boundedness of ftruef_{\rm true} and the sharpness condition imply

(ftrue−α​f)⊤​(w−w⁡(f))\displaystyle(f_{\rm true}-\alpha f)^{\top}\bigl(w-w(f)\bigr) =ftrue⊤​(w−w⁡(f))−α​f⊤​(w−w⁡(f))\displaystyle=f_{\rm true}^{\top}\bigl(w-w(f)\bigr)-\alpha f^{\top}\bigl(w-w(f)\bigr)
≤(U−α​κ)​‖w−w⁡(f)‖.\displaystyle\leq\bigl(U-\alpha\kappa\bigr)\|w-w(f)\|.

If α​κ≥U\alpha\kappa\geq U, the right-hand side is nonpositive for every w∈𝒲w\in\mathcal{W}, while choosing w=w⁡(f)w=w(f) gives zero. Hence, the maximum is zero. If α​κ<U\alpha\kappa<U, then ‖w−w⁡(f)‖≤2​Bw\|w-w(f)\|\leq 2B_{w} and U<U2/(κ​α)U<U^{2}/(\kappa\alpha), so

maxw∈𝒲⁡(ftrue−α​f)⊤​(w−w⁡(f))≤2​U2​Bwκ​α.\max_{w\in\mathcal{W}}(f_{\rm true}-\alpha f)^{\top}\bigl(w-w(f)\bigr)\leq\frac{2U^{2}B_{w}}{\kappa\alpha}.

Therefore, the same bound holds for every α>0\alpha>0.

For the second term, the optimality of w⁡(ftrue)w(f_{\rm true}) under ftruef_{\rm true} gives ftrue⊤​(w⁡(ftrue)−w⁡(f))≤0f_{\rm true}^{\top}(w(f_{\rm true})-w(f))\leq 0. Thus,

f⊤​(w⁡(ftrue)−w⁡(f))\displaystyle f^{\top}\bigl(w(f_{\rm true})-w(f)\bigr) =(f−ftrue)⊤​(w⁡(ftrue)−w⁡(f))+ftrue⊤​(w⁡(ftrue)−w⁡(f))\displaystyle=(f-f_{\rm true})^{\top}\bigl(w(f_{\rm true})-w(f)\bigr)+f_{\rm true}^{\top}\bigl(w(f_{\rm true})-w(f)\bigr)
≤2​Bw​‖f−ftrue‖.\displaystyle\leq 2B_{w}\|f-f_{\rm true}\|.

Combining the two bounds yields

ℓα​(ftrue,f)−R⁡(ftrue,f)≤2​U2​Bwκ​α+2​α​Bw​‖f−ftrue‖.\ell_{\alpha}(f_{\rm true},f)-R(f_{\rm true},f)\leq\frac{2U^{2}B_{w}}{\kappa\alpha}+2\alpha B_{w}\|f-f_{\rm true}\|.

Step 2 (Uncertainty perturbation). Using the definition of ℓα\ell_{\alpha},

ℓα​(f∗,f)−ℓα​(ftrue,f)\displaystyle\ell_{\alpha}(f^{\ast},f)-\ell_{\alpha}(f_{\rm true},f) =maxw∈𝒲⁡(f∗−α​f)⊤​w−maxw∈𝒲⁡(ftrue−α​f)⊤​w\displaystyle=\max_{w\in\mathcal{W}}(f^{\ast}-\alpha f)^{\top}w-\max_{w\in\mathcal{W}}(f_{\rm true}-\alpha f)^{\top}w
+α​f⊤​(w⁡(f∗)−w⁡(ftrue))+c⁡(ftrue)−c⁡(f∗).\displaystyle+\alpha f^{\top}\bigl(w(f^{\ast})-w(f_{\rm true})\bigr)+c(f_{\rm true})-c(f^{\ast}).

The first difference is bounded by

maxw∈𝒲⁡(f∗−α​f)⊤​w−maxw∈𝒲⁡(ftrue−α​f)⊤​w≤maxw∈𝒲⁡(f∗−ftrue)⊤​w≤Bw​‖f∗−ftrue‖.\displaystyle\max_{w\in\mathcal{W}}(f^{\ast}-\alpha f)^{\top}w-\max_{w\in\mathcal{W}}(f_{\rm true}-\alpha f)^{\top}w\leq\max_{w\in\mathcal{W}}(f^{\ast}-f_{\rm true})^{\top}w\leq B_{w}\|f^{\ast}-f_{\rm true}\|.

Similarly, since w⁡(f∗)w(f^{\ast}) is feasible under ftruef_{\rm true},

c⁡(ftrue)−c⁡(f∗)≤(ftrue−f∗)⊤​w​(f∗)≤Bw​‖f∗−ftrue‖.c(f_{\rm true})-c(f^{\ast})\leq(f_{\rm true}-f^{\ast})^{\top}w(f^{\ast})\leq B_{w}\|f^{\ast}-f_{\rm true}\|.

It remains to bound the term involving the two optimal decisions. Since w⁡(f∗)w(f^{\ast}) is optimal under f∗f^{\ast}, f∗⊤​(w⁡(f∗)−w⁡(ftrue))≤0{f^{\ast}}^{\top}(w(f^{\ast})-w(f_{\rm true}))\leq 0. Hence,

f⊤​(w⁡(f∗)−w⁡(ftrue))=(f−f∗)⊤​(w⁡(f∗)−w⁡(ftrue))+f∗⊤​(w⁡(f∗)−w⁡(ftrue))≤2​Bw​‖f∗−f‖.\displaystyle f^{\top}\bigl(w(f^{\ast})-w(f_{\rm true})\bigr)=(f-f^{\ast})^{\top}\bigl(w(f^{\ast})-w(f_{\rm true})\bigr)+{f^{\ast}}^{\top}\bigl(w(f^{\ast})-w(f_{\rm true})\bigr)\leq 2B_{w}\|f^{\ast}-f\|.

Therefore,

ℓα​(f∗,f)−ℓα​(ftrue,f)≤2​α​Bw​‖f∗−f‖+2​Bw​‖f∗−ftrue‖.\ell_{\alpha}(f^{\ast},f)-\ell_{\alpha}(f_{\rm true},f)\leq 2\alpha B_{w}\|f^{\ast}-f\|+2B_{w}\|f^{\ast}-f_{\rm true}\|.

Step 3 (Combining the bounds). Combining Steps 1 and 2 gives

ℓα​(f∗,f)−R⁡(ftrue,f)≤\displaystyle\ell_{\alpha}(f^{\ast},f)-R(f_{\rm true},f)\leq 2​U2​Bwκ​α+2​α​Bw​(‖f−ftrue‖+‖f∗−f‖)+2​Bw​‖f∗−ftrue‖,\displaystyle\frac{2U^{2}B_{w}}{\kappa\alpha}+2\alpha B_{w}\left(\|f-f_{\rm true}\|+\|f^{\ast}-f\|\right)+2B_{w}\|f^{\ast}-f_{\rm true}\|,

which proves (8).

Finally, suppose that ‖f−ftrue‖+‖f∗−f‖>0\|f-f_{\rm true}\|+\|f^{\ast}-f\|>0. The part of the bound that depends on α\alpha is

2​U2​Bwκ​α+2​α​Bw​(‖f−ftrue‖+‖f∗−f‖).\frac{2U^{2}B_{w}}{\kappa\alpha}+2\alpha B_{w}\left(\|f-f_{\rm true}\|+\|f^{\ast}-f\|\right).

Differentiating with respect to α\alpha and setting the derivative equal to zero gives

−2​U2​Bwκ​α2+2​Bw​(‖f−ftrue‖+‖f∗−f‖)=0.-\frac{2U^{2}B_{w}}{\kappa\alpha^{2}}+2B_{w}\left(\|f-f_{\rm true}\|+\|f^{\ast}-f\|\right)=0.

Solving for α\alpha yields

α∗=Uκ⁡(‖f−ftrue‖+‖f∗−f‖).\alpha^{\ast}=\frac{U}{\sqrt{\kappa\left(\|f-f_{\rm true}\|+\|f^{\ast}-f\|\right)}}.

Since the second derivative is positive for every α>0\alpha>0, this is the unique minimizer of the α\alpha-dependent part of the bound. This proves (9). □\square

Appendix E Proof of Theorem 3.3

Proof E.1

Proof. For a fixed realization ε\varepsilon, define

hε​(z):=ℓα​(f0+ε,g⁡(z)),g⁡(z)=f¯+V​z.h_{\varepsilon}(z):=\ell_{\alpha}(f_{0}+\varepsilon,g(z)),\qquad g(z)=\bar{f}+Vz.

By Proposition 3.1, ℓα​(f0+ε,⋅)\ell_{\alpha}(f_{0}+\varepsilon,\cdot) is convex. Since g⁡(z)g(z) is affine, the affine composition rule implies that hε​(z)h_{\varepsilon}(z) is convex in zz. Therefore,

ϕ⁡(z)=𝔼ε∼𝒫​[hε​(z)],\phi(z)=\mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{P}}\left[h_{\varepsilon}(z)\right],

is convex, since expectation preserves convexity. Moreover, the feasible set {z:z⊤​H​z≤r2}\{z:z^{\top}Hz\leq r^{2}\} is convex because H≻0H\succ 0. Hence, the expectation formulation is a convex optimization problem.

We next establish the subgradient expression. By Proposition 3.1, for each realization f0+εf_{0}+\varepsilon,

α⁡[w⁡(f0+ε)−w⁡(α​g​(z)−f0−ε)]∈∂fℓα​(f0+ε,g⁡(z)).\alpha\left[w(f_{0}+\varepsilon)-w\bigl(\alpha g(z)-f_{0}-\varepsilon\bigr)\right]\in\partial_{f}\ell_{\alpha}(f_{0}+\varepsilon,g(z)).

Since g⁡(z)=f¯+V​zg(z)=\bar{f}+Vz is affine, the affine subgradient chain rule gives

α​V⊤​[w⁡(f0+ε)−w⁡(α​g​(z)−f0−ε)]∈∂zhε​(z).\alpha V^{\top}\left[w(f_{0}+\varepsilon)-w\bigl(\alpha g(z)-f_{0}-\varepsilon\bigr)\right]\in\partial_{z}h_{\varepsilon}(z).

Under the stated integrability conditions, Proposition 3.23 of Royset and Wets (2021) allows the expectation and subgradient operations to be interchanged. Therefore,

𝔼ε∼𝒫​[α​V⊤​(w⁡(f0+ε)−w⁡(α​g​(z)−f0−ε))]∈∂ϕ⁡(z),\mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{P}}\left[\alpha V^{\top}\left(w(f_{0}+\varepsilon)-w\bigl(\alpha g(z)-f_{0}-\varepsilon\bigr)\right)\right]\in\partial\phi(z),

which is the subgradient expression stated in Theorem 3.3. □\square

Appendix F Extension to Alternative Risk Measures

This appendix provides the formal statement and proof of the extension mentioned in the main text, showing that the convexity and subgradient characterization also applies to the Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) formulation. Throughout this appendix, β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1) denotes the CVaR confidence level, while α>0\alpha>0 remains the scaling parameter in the surrogate loss.

Appendix G Demonstration Decision Problem

We consider a stylized investment allocation problem faced by an urban transportation authority. The authority is endowed with a fixed capital budget BB and seeks to allocate this budget across a set of candidate road segments in order to reduce aggregate commuter travel time in the city. Typical interventions include road widening, signal timing optimization, and intersection redesign, each of which improves link-level travel efficiency.

Let J={1,…,m}J=\{1,\dots,m\} denote the set of candidate road segments eligible for investment. Prior to improvement, segment j∈Jj\in J has a baseline per-traveler travel time tj0t_{j}^{0}. The city’s travel demand is represented by OD demand vector f∈ℝ+nf\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}, where fif_{i} denotes the daily travel demand associated with OD pair i∈N:={1,…,n}i\in N:=\{1,\dots,n\}. The demand vector ff is generated by an upstream prediction model and serves as the key informational input to the downstream investment allocation decision. Network connectivity between OD pairs and road segments is described by a binary incidence matrix S∈{0,1}n×mS\in\{0,1\}^{n\times m}, where Si​j=1S_{ij}=1 if OD pair ii traverses segment jj, and Si​j=0S_{ij}=0 otherwise. We abstract from endogenous route choice and network equilibrium effects. Each OD pair is assumed to follow a representative baseline path, and link-level improvements are aggregated along this fixed path to obtain OD-level travel time. For each road segment j∈Jj\in J, let xjx_{j} denote the expected reduction (in minutes) in per-traveler travel time achieved through investment on that segment. We impose an upper bound uju_{j} reflecting engineering or physical feasibility constraints, here uj≤tj0u_{j}\leq t_{j}^{0}. Let wiw_{i} denote the per trip travel time for OD pair ii as a result of the investments. Let cjc_{j} denote the marginal cost of reducing one unit (minute) of travel time on segment jj. Thus, the total investment cost on segment jj equals cj​xjc_{j}x_{j}, and the aggregate expenditure across all segments must not exceed the available budget BB. The sets, parameters, and decision variables are summarized in Table 2

The transportation authority seeks to minimize the total system-wide travel time experienced by all commuters. Because fif_{i} represents the demand for OD pair ii, the aggregate daily travel time equals ∑i∈Nfi​wi\sum_{i\in N}f_{i}w_{i}. The resulting linear program is:

minx,w\displaystyle\min_{x,w}\quad ∑i∈Nfi​wi\displaystyle\sum_{i\in N}f_{i}w_{i} (16)
s.t. wi=∑j∈JSi​j​(tj0−xj),\displaystyle w_{i}=\sum_{j\in J}S_{ij}(t_{j}^{0}-x_{j}), ∀i∈N,\displaystyle\forall i\in N, (17)
∑j∈Jcj​xj≤B,\displaystyle\sum_{j\in J}c_{j}x_{j}\leq B, (18)
0≤xj≤uj,\displaystyle 0\leq x_{j}\leq u_{j}, ∀j∈J.\displaystyle\forall j\in J. (19)

Constraint (17) defines the post investment travel time for each OD pair as the sum of the improved link travel times along its route. Constraint (18) enforces the budget limitation. Constraint (19) ensures feasibility of link-level improvements. This formulation captures a fundamental trade-off in transportation planning: investments on heavily utilized corridors yield large aggregate benefits, yet marginal improvement costs and physical constraints limit achievable reductions.

Appendix H Supplementary Details for Experiment 4.2

H.1 Feature and OD Flow Generation

For each experimental instance, we generate synthetic OD-flow samples from a nonlinear feature-to-demand mapping. Each sample is associated with a feature vector xi∈ℝdfeatx_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{feat}}}, where dfeat=4d_{\mathrm{feat}}=4. The first three feature dimensions are independently drawn from a standard normal distribution, while the fourth dimension is a binary indicator:

xi​1,xi​2,xi​3∼𝒩⁡(0,1),xi​4∼Bernoulli⁡(0.5).x_{i1},x_{i2},x_{i3}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1),\qquad x_{i4}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(0.5).

Training and testing feature vectors are generated independently using different random seeds.

Let nODn_{\mathrm{OD}} denote the number of OD pairs. For a given polynomial order P∈{1,…,6}P\in\{1,\ldots,6\}, the latent OD-flow vector is generated by

Zi=b+xi​W1⊤+∑p=2Pxi∘p​Wp⊤,Z_{i}=b+x_{i}W_{1}^{\top}+\sum_{p=2}^{P}x_{i}^{\circ p}W_{p}^{\top},

where xi∘px_{i}^{\circ p} denotes the elementwise pp-th power of the feature vector.

The nonlinear mapping is parameterized so that lower-order terms capture the dominant feature effects, while higher-order terms introduce progressively smaller nonlinear perturbations. Specifically, for each experimental instance, we first draw an intercept vector b∈ℝnODb\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\mathrm{OD}}} and a collection of coefficient matrices {Wp}p=1P\{W_{p}\}_{p=1}^{P}, where Wp∈ℝnOD×dfeatW_{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\mathrm{OD}}\times d_{\mathrm{feat}}}. The entries are sampled independently according to

bj∼U⁡(0,3),(Wp)j​k∼U⁡(−ρp,ρp),b_{j}\sim U(0,3),\qquad(W_{p})_{jk}\sim U(-\rho_{p},\rho_{p}),

with

(ρ1,ρ2,ρ3,ρ4,ρ5,ρ6)=(1, 0.5, 0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.02).(\rho_{1},\rho_{2},\rho_{3},\rho_{4},\rho_{5},\rho_{6})=(1,\;0.5,\;0.2,\;0.1,\;0.05,\;0.02).

Only the matrices W1,…,WPW_{1},\ldots,W_{P} are used for a polynomial order PP. This scaling prevents high-order polynomial terms from dominating the generated OD flows, while still allowing the true demand function to become increasingly nonlinear as PP increases.

Given the latent value ZiZ_{i}, the clean OD-flow vector is constructed through a softplus transformation, Q~i=log⁡(1+exp⁡(Zi))\widetilde{Q}_{i}=\log(1+\exp(Z_{i})), which ensures nonnegativity. The transformed values are then rescaled to the target OD-flow magnitude and truncated to a bounded interval:

Qi=Π[0,2000]​(s​Q~i),Q_{i}=\Pi_{[0,2000]}\left(s\,\widetilde{Q}_{i}\right),

where s>0s>0 is a fixed scaling constant and Π[0,2000]​(⋅)\Pi_{[0,2000]}(\cdot) denotes componentwise projection onto the interval [0,2000][0,2000]. This step keeps the generated OD flows on a stable numerical scale and avoids unrealistically large demands induced by rare high-order polynomial values. The scaling factor places the OD flows on a realistic numerical scale for the downstream investment problem, while the clipping step avoids unrealistically large demands caused by rare high-order polynomial values.

Appendix I Supplementary Details for Experiment 4.3

I.1 OD Demand Patterns Generation

Common construction.

Let m∈{1,…,5}m\in\{1,\ldots,5\} index the five demand-generation modes. For each OD pair (i,j)(i,j), let di​jd_{ij} denote the shortest-path distance, normalized by the median of all positive shortest-path distances in the network. For each mode mm, we first construct a base OD pattern

F~(m)=(1−λ)​B+λ​S(m),λ=0.85,\widetilde{F}^{(m)}=(1-\lambda)B+\lambda S^{(m)},\qquad\lambda=0.85,

where BB is a common nonnegative gravity-type background and S(m)S^{(m)} is the nonnegative mode-specific component.

The common background BB incorporates heterogeneous origin-production and destination-attraction effects, moderate distance decay, and mild cell-level variation. It introduces a shared level of spatial heterogeneity across all modes and prevents the resulting OD patterns from becoming artificially sparse. The larger weight on S(m)S^{(m)} preserves the distinctive structure of each demand-generation mode. Intrazonal demand is set to zero.

Pattern variants.

As illustrated in Figure 11, the five mode-specific components S(m)S^{(m)} are constructed as follows.

  1. 1.

    Distance decay. Demand is generated from heterogeneous origin and destination propensities and decreases exponentially with network distance. This pattern represents a conventional gravity-type structure in which nearby OD pairs interact more strongly.

  2. 2.

    Low-rank latent demand. The demand signal is obtained from the nonnegative part of a rank-three bilinear factor model and is moderately attenuated by distance. This construction captures correlated OD movements driven by a small number of latent factors.

  3. 3.

    Community blocks. Nodes are randomly assigned to three communities, with substantially stronger demand within communities than across communities. Cell-level variation is retained so that flows remain heterogeneous within each block.

  4. 4.

    Directional corridors. Disjoint source and sink sets, each containing approximately one quarter of the nodes, are selected to form dominant source-to-sink corridors. Corridor demand decreases with distance, while a weak diffuse component allows residual demand outside the primary corridors, producing a strongly asymmetric OD structure.

  5. 5.

    Hub–spoke concentration. The node with the highest network degree is designated as the hub. Demand is concentrated on trips originating from or terminating at the hub, with a small residual component representing interactions among nonhub nodes.

Demand scenarios.

Let ℓ∈{1,2,3}\ell\in\{1,2,3\} index the low, medium, and high demand levels, with prescribed aggregate demands Qℓ∈{1,000, 10,000, 20,000}Q_{\ell}\in\{1{,}000,\;10{,}000,\;20{,}000\}, respectively. Combining the five demand-generation modes with the three demand levels yields 15 scenarios.

To ensure that the three levels are not simple scalar copies of the same OD pattern, we introduce level-specific origin and destination effects. For each level ℓ\ell, define

Mi​j(ℓ)=exp⁡(αi(ℓ)+βj(ℓ)),M_{ij}^{(\ell)}=\exp\left(\alpha_{i}^{(\ell)}+\beta_{j}^{(\ell)}\right),

where αi(ℓ)\alpha_{i}^{(\ell)} and βj(ℓ)\beta_{j}^{(\ell)} denote the origin- and destination-specific effects, respectively. The effects are centered, while their dispersion varies across demand levels.

The ground-truth OD matrix for mode mm and demand level ℓ\ell is then constructed as

Ftrue(m,ℓ)=ScaleQℓ⁡(F~(m)⊙M(ℓ)),F_{\mathrm{true}}^{(m,\ell)}=\operatorname{Scale}_{Q_{\ell}}\left(\widetilde{F}^{(m)}\odot M^{(\ell)}\right),

where ⊙\odot denotes elementwise multiplication and, for any nonnegative matrix AA with zero diagonal,

ScaleQ⁡(A)=Q∑i≠jAi​j​A.\operatorname{Scale}_{Q}(A)=\frac{Q}{\sum_{i\neq j}A_{ij}}A.

Hence, ∑i≠jFtrue,i​j(m,ℓ)=Qℓ\sum_{i\neq j}F_{\mathrm{true},ij}^{(m,\ell)}=Q_{\ell}.

For each demand level ℓ\ell, the same multiplier M(ℓ)M^{(\ell)} is applied across all five modes, and fixed random seeds are used throughout. This design preserves comparability across modes while allowing both aggregate demand and OD margins to vary across demand levels.

Finally, each ground-truth OD matrix is vectorized as ftrue(m,ℓ)f_{\mathrm{true}}^{(m,\ell)} and mapped to link flows through the common assignment relation

L(m,ℓ)=X​ftrue(m,ℓ).L^{(m,\ell)}=Xf_{\mathrm{true}}^{(m,\ell)}.

Thus, all scenarios share the same network topology and assignment mechanism, while varying only in their OD structure and demand level.

I.2 Repeated-Sampling Robustness Analysis

To examine whether the conclusions from the Sioux Falls experiment are robust to variation across experimental realizations, we conduct an additional repeated-sampling analysis. Each of the 15 demand-level–mode combinations is independently evaluated over 20 experimental realizations generated using distinct random seeds. Table 3 reports the sample mean and sample standard deviation of decision regret across these realizations.

The repeated-sampling results provide consistent evidence for the advantage of decision aware estimation. In every one of the 15 demand-level–mode combinations, both D-FULL-G and D-GEO-G achieve strictly lower mean decision regret than PTO, with no exception across the three demand levels or the five demand modes. Relative to PTO, the reduction in mean regret ranges from 55.6%55.6\% to 88.6%88.6\% for D-FULL-G and from 50.4%50.4\% to 88.6%88.6\% for D-GEO-G. Averaged across all settings, mean regret decreases from 157.28157.28 under PTO to 33.2533.25 under D-FULL-G and 33.1833.18 under D-GEO-G, corresponding to an average reduction of approximately 78.9%78.9\% for either variant. The improvement is also reflected in the variability across experimental realizations: both DWE variants have a smaller sample standard deviation than PTO in all 15 settings. For example, under high-demand Community Blocks, PTO produces a mean regret of 619.09619.09 with a standard deviation of 430.08430.08, whereas both D-FULL-G and D-GEO-G reduce these values to 98.4798.47 and 78.0078.00, respectively. Similarly, under medium-demand Directional Corridor, D-FULL-G and D-GEO-G reduce the PTO mean regret from 119.44119.44 to 53.0153.01 and 59.2659.26, while their standard deviations decrease from 143.96143.96 to 69.3569.35 and 78.9678.96. Thus, the gains from decision aware estimation are not limited to lower average regret; they are accompanied by consistently lower variation across repeated realizations. The comparison between the two DWE variants does not indicate uniform dominance. D-GEO-G achieves lower mean regret than D-FULL-G in five settings, matches it in five settings, and has higher mean regret in the remaining five, while their overall averages remain nearly identical. Its largest relative improvement occurs under medium-demand Distance Decay, where mean regret decreases from 14.9214.92 to 12.0412.04, a reduction of 19.3%19.3\% relative to D-FULL-G. Its largest absolute shortfall occurs under medium-demand Directional Corridor, where mean regret increases from 53.0153.01 to 59.2659.26; nevertheless, D-GEO-G still achieves a strictly lower mean regret than PTO by 50.4%50.4\% in this setting. These differences reflect the trade-off introduced by the geometric restriction. D-FULL-G permits a more flexible adjustment, whereas D-GEO-G restricts the admissible adjustment through the radius rr. This restriction can limit sample-specific over-adjustment, but it may also exclude corrections that are important to the downstream decision and thereby introduce approximation error. Notably, the selected radius reaches r∗=10r^{\ast}=10, the maximum radius considered, in all five settings where D-GEO-G has higher mean regret than D-FULL-G. This boundary behavior is consistent with the admissible geometric region remaining too restrictive in these cases. The underperformance is concentrated in the Low Rank, Directional Corridor, and Hub Spoke modes, whose global, directional, or hub-centered structures may be less well represented by a finite geometric neighborhood. Although this observation does not establish that increasing rmaxr_{\max} would necessarily eliminate the performance gap, it identifies the finite geometric restriction as a plausible source of approximation error. D-GEO-G should therefore be interpreted as a regularized alternative to D-FULL-G rather than as a uniformly dominating variant. Importantly, its occasional disadvantage relative to D-FULL-G does not affect the central robustness conclusion: D-GEO-G, like D-FULL-G, achieves strictly lower mean regret and lower cross-realization variability than PTO in every tested setting.
